**Medical sociology** is the [sociological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociological "Sociological") analysis of [health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health "Health"), illness, differential access to medical resources, the social [organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organization "Organization") of [medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicine "Medicine"), Health Care Delivery, the production of medical knowledge, selection of methods, the study of [actions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_actions "Social actions") and interactions of [healthcare professionals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_professional "Health professional"), and the social or cultural (rather than clinical or bodily) effects of medical practice.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-2) The field commonly interacts with the [sociology of knowledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociology_of_knowledge "Sociology of knowledge"), [science and technology studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_and_technology_studies "Science and technology studies"), and [social epistemology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_epistemology "Social epistemology"). Medical sociologists are also interested in the qualitative experiences of patients, doctors, and medical education; often working at the boundaries of [public health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_health "Public health"), [social work](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_work "Social work"), [demography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demography "Demography") and [gerontology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerontology "Gerontology") to explore phenomena at the intersection of the social and clinical sciences. [Health disparities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_disparities "Health disparities") commonly relate to typical categories such as [class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_class "Social class"), [race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(classification_of_human_beings) "Race (classification of human beings)"), [ethnicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnicity "Ethnicity"), [immigration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immigration "Immigration"), [gender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gender "Gender"), [sexuality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexuality "Sexuality"), and age. Objective sociological research findings quickly become a [normative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normative "Normative") and [political](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political "Political") issue.

Early work in medical sociology was conducted by [Lawrence J Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Joseph_Henderson "Lawrence Joseph Henderson") whose theoretical interests in the work of [Vilfredo Pareto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vilfredo_Pareto "Vilfredo Pareto") inspired [Talcott Parsons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talcott_Parsons "Talcott Parsons")' interests in [sociological systems theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systems_theory#Sociology_and_Sociocybernetics "Systems theory"). Parsons was one of the early leaders in medical sociology, and applied [social role](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_role "Social role") theory to interactional relations between sick people and others. Later other sociologists such as [Eliot Freidson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Profession_of_Medicine "Profession of Medicine") have taken a [conflict theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conflict_theories "Conflict theories") perspective, looking at how the medical profession secures its own interests.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:8-3):291 Key contributors to medical sociology since the 1950s include [Howard S. Becker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_S._Becker "Howard S. Becker"), [Mike Bury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Bury "Michael Bury"), [Peter Conrad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Conrad_(sociologist) "Peter Conrad (sociologist)"), Jack Douglas, [Eliot Freidson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliot_Freidson "Eliot Freidson"), David Silverman, Phil Strong, [Bernice Pescosolido](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernice_A._Pescosolido "Bernice A. Pescosolido"), [Carl May](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_May "Carl May"), Anne Rogers, [Anselm Strauss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anselm_Strauss "Anselm Strauss"), [Renee Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renee_Fox "Renee Fox"), and Joseph W. Schneider.

The field of medical sociology is usually taught as part of a wider [sociology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociology "Sociology"), [clinical psychology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinical_psychology "Clinical psychology") or [health studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_sciences "Health sciences") degree course, or on dedicated master's degree courses where it is sometimes combined with the study of [medical ethics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_ethics "Medical ethics") and [bioethics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bioethics "Bioethics"). In Britain, sociology was introduced into the medical curriculum following the Goodenough report in 1944: "In medicine, 'social explanations' of the [etiology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etiology "Etiology") of disease meant for some doctors a redirection of medical thought from the purely clinical and psychological criteria of illness. The introduction of 'social' factors into medical explanation was most strongly evidenced in branches of medicine closely related to the community — Social Medicine and, later, General Practice".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-4)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Samuel W. Bloom argues that the study of medical sociology has a long history but tended to be done as one of advocacy in response to social events rather than a field of study. He cites the 1842 publication of the sanitary conditions of the labouring population of Great Britain as a good example of such research. This medical sociology included an element of [social science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_science "Social science"), studying social structures as a cause or mediating factor in disease, such as for [public health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_health "Public health") or [social medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_medicine "Social medicine").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:0-5):11

Bloom argues the development of medical sociology is linked to the development of sociology within American universities. He argues that the 1865 creation of the [American Social Science Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Social_Science_Association "American Social Science Association") (ASSA) was a key event in this development.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:0-5):25 ASSA's initial aim was policy reform on the basis of science.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:0-5):25 Bloom argues that over the next few decades the role of ASSA moved from advocacy to academic discipline, noting that a number of academic professional bodies broke away from the ASSA during this period, starting with the [American Historical Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Historical_Association "American Historical Association") in 1884. The [American Sociological Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Sociological_Association "American Sociological Association") formed in 1905.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:0-5):26

The [Russell Sage Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Sage_Foundation "Russell Sage Foundation"), formed in 1907, was a large philanthropic organization which worked closely with the American Sociological Society, which had medical sociology as a primary focus of its suggested policy reform.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:0-5):36 Bloom argues that the presidency of Donald R Young, a professor of sociology, that started in 1947 was significant in the development of medical sociology.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:0-5):182 Young motivated by a desire to legitimize sociology, encouraged [Esther Lucile Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esther_Lucile_Brown "Esther Lucile Brown"), an anthropologist who studied the professions, to focus her work on the medical professions due to medicine's societal status.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:0-5):183

### Harry Stock Sullivan

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Harry Stock Sullivan")]

[Harry Stack Sullivan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Stack_Sullivan "Harry Stack Sullivan") was a psychiatrist who investigated the treatment of [schizophrenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schizophrenia "Schizophrenia") using approaches of [interpersonal psychotherapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interpersonal_psychotherapy "Interpersonal psychotherapy") working with sociologists and social scientists including [Lawrence K. Frank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_K._Frank "Lawrence K. Frank"), [W. I. Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._I._Thomas "W. I. Thomas"), [Ruth Benedict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Benedict "Ruth Benedict"), [Harold Lasswell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Lasswell "Harold Lasswell") and [Edward Sapir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Sapir "Edward Sapir").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:0-5):76 Bloom argues that Sullivans work, and its focus on putative interpersonal causes and treatment of schizophrenia influenced [ethnographic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnography "Ethnography") study of the hospital setting.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:0-5):76

## Medical profession

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Medical profession")]

The [profession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Profession "Profession") of [medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicine "Medicine") has been studied by sociologists. [Talcott Parsons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talcott_Parsons "Talcott Parsons") looked at the profession from a [functionalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structural_functionalism "Structural functionalism") perspective, focusing on medics roles as [experts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expert "Expert"), their altruism, and how they support communities. Other sociologists have taken a [conflict theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conflict_theories "Conflict theories") perspective, looking at how the medical profession secures its own interests. Of these, [Marxist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marxism "Marxism") conflict theory perspective considers how the ruling classes can enact power through medicine, while other theories propose a more [structural pluralist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structural_pluralism "Structural pluralism") approach, exemplified by [Eliot Freidson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliot_Freidson "Eliot Freidson"), looking at how the professions themselves secure influence.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:8-3):291

### Medical education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Medical education")]

The study of [medical education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_education "Medical education") has been a central part of medical sociology since its emergence in the 1950s. The first publication on the topic was Robert Merton's _The Student Physician_. Other scholars who studied the field include [Howard S. Becker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_S._Becker "Howard S. Becker"), with his publication _Boys in White_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:9-6):1

The [hidden curriculum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hidden_curriculum "Hidden curriculum") is a concept in medical education that refers to a distinction between what is officially taught and what is learned by a medical student.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:9-6):16 The concept was introduced by [Philip W. Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_W._Jackson "Philip W. Jackson") in his book _Life in the Classroom_, but developed further by Benson Snyder. The concept has been criticised by Lakomski and there has been considerable debate on the concepts within the educational community.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:9-6):17

### Medical dominance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Medical dominance")]

Writing the 1970s, [Eliot Freidson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliot_Freidson "Eliot Freidson") argued that medicine had reached a point of "professional dominance" over the content of their work, other health professions and their clients by convincing the public of medicine's effectiveness, gaining a legal monopoly over their work, and appropriating other "medical" knowledge through control of training.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:10-7):433 This concept of dominance has been extended to professions as a whole in closure theory, where professions are seen as competing for [scope of practice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scope_of_practice "Scope of practice"), for example in the work of [Andrew Abbott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Abbott_(sociologist) "Andrew Abbott (sociologist)").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:10-7):434 Coburn argues that academic interest in medical dominance has decreased over time due to the increased role of [capitalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitalism "Capitalism") in healthcare in the US,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:10-7):436 challenges to the control of [health policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_policy "Health policy") by [politicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politician "Politician"), [economists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economist "Economist") and planners, and increased agency of [patients](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patient "Patient") through access to the internet.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:10-7):439 Sociologist nursing professor [Kath M. Melia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kath_M._Melia "Kath M. Melia") argues that so far as nurses are concerned, medical paternalistic attitudes have remained.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-9)

## Medicalization

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Medicalization")]

_[Medicalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicalization "Medicalization")_ describes the process whereby an ever-wider range of human experiences are defined, experienced and treated as a medical condition. Examples of medicalization can be seen in [deviance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deviance_(sociology) "Deviance (sociology)"), such as defining [addiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addiction "Addiction") or [antisocial personality disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisocial_personality_disorder "Antisocial personality disorder") as a medical condition. Feminist scholars have shown that the female body is prone to medicalization, arguing that the tendency of viewing the female body as the [Other](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Other_(philosophy) "Other (philosophy)") has been a factor in this.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:6-10):151

Medicalization can obscure social factors by defining a condition as existing entirely within an individual and can be depoliticizing, suggesting than an intervention should be medical when the best intervention is political. Medicalization can give the profession of medicine undue influence.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:6-10):152

## Social construction of illness

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Social construction of illness")]

See also: [Social construction of disability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_construction_of_disability "Social construction of disability")

Social constructionists study the relationships between ideas about [illness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illness "Illness") and expression, perception and understanding of illness by individuals, institutions and society.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:6-10):148 Social constructionists study why diseases exist in one place and not another, or disappear from a particular area. For example, [premenstrual syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premenstrual_syndrome "Premenstrual syndrome"), [anorexia nervosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anorexia_nervosa "Anorexia nervosa") and [susto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susto "Susto") appear to exist in some cultures but not others.

There are a broad range of social constructionist frameworks used in medical sociology that make different assumptions about the relationships between ideas, social processes and the material world.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:6-10):149 Illnesses vary in the degree to which their definition is socially constructed; some illnesses are straightforwardly biological.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:6-10):150 For straightforwardly biological diseases, it would not be meaningful to describe them as a social construction, though it might be meaningful to study the social processes that resulted in the discovery of the disease.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:6-10):150

Some illnesses are contested when a patient complains about a disease despite the medical community being unable to find a biological mechanism for disease. Examples of contested diseases include [myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myalgic_encephalomyelitis/chronic_fatigue_syndrome "Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome") (ME/CFS), [fibromyalgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibromyalgia "Fibromyalgia") and [Gulf War syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_War_syndrome "Gulf War syndrome"). Contested diseases can be studied as social constructs but there is no biomedical understanding. Some contested diseases, such as ME/CFS, are accepted by the institutions of biomedicine while others, such as [environmental diseases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_disease "Environmental disease"), are not.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:6-10):153

### Sick role

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Sick role")]

The study of the social construction of illness within medical sociology can be traced to [Talcott Parsons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talcott_Parsons "Talcott Parsons")' notion of the [sick role](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sick_role "Sick role").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:6-10):148 Parsons introduced the notion of the sick role in his book _The Social System._[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:1-11):211 Parsons argued that the sick role is a social role approved and enforced by [social norms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_norm "Social norm") and institutional behaviours where an individual is viewed as showing certain behaviour because they are in need of support.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:1-11):212

Parsons argues that defining properties are that the sick person is exempt from normal social roles, that they are not "responsible" for their condition, that they should try to get well, and that they should seek technically competent people to help them.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:1-11):213

The concept of the sick role has been critiqued by sociologists from neo-marxist, phenomonological and social interactionist perspectives, as well as by those with anti-establishment viewpoints.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:2-12):76 Burnham argues that part of this criticism is a rejection of [functionalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structural_functionalism "Structural functionalism") due to its associations with conservatism. The sick role fell out of favour in the 1990s.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:2-12)

### Labelling theory

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Labelling theory")]

[Labelling theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labeling_theory "Labeling theory") is derived from the work of [Howard S. Becker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_S._Becker "Howard S. Becker"), who studied the sociology of marijuana use. He argued that norms and deviant behaviour are partly the result of the definitions applied by others. [Eliot Freidson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliot_Freidson "Eliot Freidson") applied these concepts to illness.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:1-11):226

Labelling theory separates the aspects of an individual's behaviour caused by an illness, and that which is caused by the application of a label. Freidson distinguished labels based on legitimacy and the degree to which to this legitimacy affected an individual's responsibilities.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:1-11):227

Labelling theory has been criticized on the grounds that it does not explain which behaviours are labelled as deviant and why people engage in behaviours which are labelled as deviant: labelling theory is not a complete theory of deviant behaviour.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:1-11):228

### Mental health

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Mental health")]

An illness framework is the dominant framework for disease in psychiatry and [diagnosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diagnosis "Diagnosis") is considered worthwhile.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:7-13):2 Psychiatry has emphasized the biological when considering mental illness.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:7-13):3 Some psychiatrists have criticized this model: some prefer [biopsychosocial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biopsychosocial_model "Biopsychosocial model") definitions, while others prefer [social constructionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_constructionism "Social constructionism") models, and still others have argued that madness is an intelligent response if all circumstances are understood ([Laing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R.D._Laing "R.D. Laing") and [Esterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Esterson "Aaron Esterson")). [Thomas Szasz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Szasz "Thomas Szasz"), who trained as a psychiatrist, argued that mental health was a bad concept in his 1961 book _[The Myth of Mental Illness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Myth\_of\_Mental\_Illness "The Myth of Mental Illness")_, arguing that minds can only be ill metaphorically.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:7-13):3

## Doctor–patient relationship

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Doctor–patient relationship")]

The [doctor–patient relationship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor%E2%80%93patient_relationship "Doctor–patient relationship"), the social interactions between healthcare providers and those who interact with them, is studied by medical sociology. There are different models for the interaction between a patient and doctor, which may have been more or less prevalent at different times. One such model is medical consumerism, which has partly given way to [patient consumerism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patient_consumerism?action=edit&redlink=1 "Patient consumerism (page does not exist)").

### Medical paternalism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Medical paternalism")]

[Medical paternalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_paternalism "Medical paternalism") is the perspective that doctors want what is best for the patient and must take decisions on behalf of the patient because the patient is not competent to make their own decisions. Parsons argued that though there was an asymmetry of knowledge and power in the doctor–patient relationship, the medical system provided sufficient safeguards to protect the patient, justifying a paternalistic role by the doctor and medical system.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:3-14):496

A system of medical paternalism was prominent following the second world war through to the mid-1960s. Writing in the 1970s, Eliot Freidson referred to medicine as having "professional dominance", determining its work and defining a conceptualization of the problems that are brought to it and the best solutions to them.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:3-14):497 Professional dominance is defined by three characteristics: practitioners having power over clients, for example through dependency, knowledge, or location asymmetry; control over juniors in the field, requiring juniors' deference and submission; and control over other professions either by excluding them from practice, or placing them under control of the medical profession.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:7-13):161

Yeyoung Oh Nelson argues that this system of paternalism was in part undermined by organizational change in the following decades in the US whereby insurance companies, managers and the pharmaceutical industry started competing for role of conceptualizing and delivering medical services, part of the motive being cost-saving.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:3-14):498

## Bioethics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Bioethics")]

Main article: [Bioethics §Medical sociology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bioethics#Medical_sociology "Bioethics")

[Bioethics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bioethics "Bioethics") studies ethical concern in medical treatment and research. Many scholars believe that bioethics arose due to a perceived lack of accountability of the medical profession, the field has been broadly adopted with most US hospitals offering some form of ethical consultation. The social effects of the field of bioethics have been studied by medical sociologists.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-15):2[Informed consent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Informed_consent#Medical_sociology "Informed consent"), having its roots in bioethics, is the process by which a doctor and a patient agree to a particular intervention. Medical sociology studies the social processes that influence and at times limit consent.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-16)

## Related fields

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Related fields")]

### Social medicine

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Social medicine")]

[Social medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_medicine "Social medicine") is a similar field to medical sociology in that it tries to conceptualize social interactions[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:4-17):241 in investigating how the study of social interactions can be used in medicine.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-18):9 However, the two fields have different training, career paths, titles, funding and publication.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:4-17):241 In the 2010s, Rose and Callard argued that this distinction may be arbitrary.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:4-17):242

In the 1950s, Strauss argued that it was important to maintain the independence of medical sociology from medicine so that there was a different perspective on sociology separate from the aims of medicine.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:4-17):242 Strauss feared that if medical sociology started to adopt the goals expected by medicine it risked losing its focus on analysing society. These fears that have been echoed since by Reid, Gold and Timmermans.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:4-17):248 Rosenfeld argues that the study of sociology focused solely on making recommendations for medicine has limited use for theory building and its findings cease to apply in different social situations.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:4-17):249

Richard Boulton argues that medical sociology and social medicine are "co-produced" in the sense that social medicine responds to the conceptualization of medical practices created by medical sociology and alters medical practice and medical understanding in response, and that the effects of these changes are then analyzed by medical sociology once again.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:4-17):245 He argues that the tendency to view certain theories such as the scientific method ([positivism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positivism "Positivism")) as the basis for all knowledge, and conversely the tendency to view all knowledge as associated with some activity both risk undermining the field of medical sociology.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:4-17):250

### Medical anthropology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Medical anthropology")]

[Peter Conrad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Conrad_(sociologist) "Peter Conrad (sociologist)") notes that [medical anthropology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_anthropology "Medical anthropology") studies some of the same phenomena as medical sociology but argues that medical anthropology has different origins, originally studying medicine within non-western cultures and using different methodologies.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:5-19):91–92 He argues that there was some convergence between the disciplines, as medical sociology started to adopt some of the methodologies of anthropology such as [qualitative research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qualitative_research "Qualitative research") and began to focus more on the patient, and medical anthropology started to focus on western medicine. He argues that more interdisciplinary communication could improve both disciplines.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:5-19):97

**Medical sociology** is the [sociological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociological "Sociological") analysis of [health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health "Health"), illness, differential access to medical resources, the social [organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organization "Organization") of [medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicine "Medicine"), Health Care Delivery, the production of medical knowledge, selection of methods, the study of [actions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_actions "Social actions") and interactions of [healthcare professionals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_professional "Health professional"), and the social or cultural (rather than clinical or bodily) effects of medical practice.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-2) The field commonly interacts with the [sociology of knowledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociology_of_knowledge "Sociology of knowledge"), [science and technology studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_and_technology_studies "Science and technology studies"), and [social epistemology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_epistemology "Social epistemology"). Medical sociologists are also interested in the qualitative experiences of patients, doctors, and medical education; often working at the boundaries of [public health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_health "Public health"), [social work](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_work "Social work"), [demography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demography "Demography") and [gerontology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerontology "Gerontology") to explore phenomena at the intersection of the social and clinical sciences. [Health disparities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_disparities "Health disparities") commonly relate to typical categories such as [class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_class "Social class"), [race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_(classification_of_human_beings) "Race (classification of human beings)"), [ethnicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnicity "Ethnicity"), [immigration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immigration "Immigration"), [gender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gender "Gender"), [sexuality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexuality "Sexuality"), and age. Objective sociological research findings quickly become a [normative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normative "Normative") and [political](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political "Political") issue.

Early work in medical sociology was conducted by [Lawrence J Henderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Joseph_Henderson "Lawrence Joseph Henderson") whose theoretical interests in the work of [Vilfredo Pareto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vilfredo_Pareto "Vilfredo Pareto") inspired [Talcott Parsons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talcott_Parsons "Talcott Parsons")' interests in [sociological systems theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systems_theory#Sociology_and_Sociocybernetics "Systems theory"). Parsons was one of the early leaders in medical sociology, and applied [social role](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_role "Social role") theory to interactional relations between sick people and others. Later other sociologists such as [Eliot Freidson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Profession_of_Medicine "Profession of Medicine") have taken a [conflict theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conflict_theories "Conflict theories") perspective, looking at how the medical profession secures its own interests.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:8-3):291 Key contributors to medical sociology since the 1950s include [Howard S. Becker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_S._Becker "Howard S. Becker"), [Mike Bury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Bury "Michael Bury"), [Peter Conrad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Conrad_(sociologist) "Peter Conrad (sociologist)"), Jack Douglas, [Eliot Freidson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliot_Freidson "Eliot Freidson"), David Silverman, Phil Strong, [Bernice Pescosolido](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernice_A._Pescosolido "Bernice A. Pescosolido"), [Carl May](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_May "Carl May"), Anne Rogers, [Anselm Strauss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anselm_Strauss "Anselm Strauss"), [Renee Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renee_Fox "Renee Fox"), and Joseph W. Schneider.

The field of medical sociology is usually taught as part of a wider [sociology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociology "Sociology"), [clinical psychology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinical_psychology "Clinical psychology") or [health studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_sciences "Health sciences") degree course, or on dedicated master's degree courses where it is sometimes combined with the study of [medical ethics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_ethics "Medical ethics") and [bioethics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bioethics "Bioethics"). In Britain, sociology was introduced into the medical curriculum following the Goodenough report in 1944: "In medicine, 'social explanations' of the [etiology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etiology "Etiology") of disease meant for some doctors a redirection of medical thought from the purely clinical and psychological criteria of illness. The introduction of 'social' factors into medical explanation was most strongly evidenced in branches of medicine closely related to the community — Social Medicine and, later, General Practice".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-4)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Samuel W. Bloom argues that the study of medical sociology has a long history but tended to be done as one of advocacy in response to social events rather than a field of study. He cites the 1842 publication of the sanitary conditions of the labouring population of Great Britain as a good example of such research. This medical sociology included an element of [social science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_science "Social science"), studying social structures as a cause or mediating factor in disease, such as for [public health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_health "Public health") or [social medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_medicine "Social medicine").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:0-5):11

Bloom argues the development of medical sociology is linked to the development of sociology within American universities. He argues that the 1865 creation of the [American Social Science Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Social_Science_Association "American Social Science Association") (ASSA) was a key event in this development.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:0-5):25 ASSA's initial aim was policy reform on the basis of science.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:0-5):25 Bloom argues that over the next few decades the role of ASSA moved from advocacy to academic discipline, noting that a number of academic professional bodies broke away from the ASSA during this period, starting with the [American Historical Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Historical_Association "American Historical Association") in 1884. The [American Sociological Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Sociological_Association "American Sociological Association") formed in 1905.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:0-5):26

The [Russell Sage Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Sage_Foundation "Russell Sage Foundation"), formed in 1907, was a large philanthropic organization which worked closely with the American Sociological Society, which had medical sociology as a primary focus of its suggested policy reform.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:0-5):36 Bloom argues that the presidency of Donald R Young, a professor of sociology, that started in 1947 was significant in the development of medical sociology.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:0-5):182 Young motivated by a desire to legitimize sociology, encouraged [Esther Lucile Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esther_Lucile_Brown "Esther Lucile Brown"), an anthropologist who studied the professions, to focus her work on the medical professions due to medicine's societal status.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:0-5):183

### Harry Stock Sullivan

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Harry Stock Sullivan")]

[Harry Stack Sullivan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Stack_Sullivan "Harry Stack Sullivan") was a psychiatrist who investigated the treatment of [schizophrenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schizophrenia "Schizophrenia") using approaches of [interpersonal psychotherapy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interpersonal_psychotherapy "Interpersonal psychotherapy") working with sociologists and social scientists including [Lawrence K. Frank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_K._Frank "Lawrence K. Frank"), [W. I. Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._I._Thomas "W. I. Thomas"), [Ruth Benedict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Benedict "Ruth Benedict"), [Harold Lasswell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Lasswell "Harold Lasswell") and [Edward Sapir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Sapir "Edward Sapir").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:0-5):76 Bloom argues that Sullivans work, and its focus on putative interpersonal causes and treatment of schizophrenia influenced [ethnographic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnography "Ethnography") study of the hospital setting.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:0-5):76

## Medical profession

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Medical profession")]

The [profession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Profession "Profession") of [medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicine "Medicine") has been studied by sociologists. [Talcott Parsons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talcott_Parsons "Talcott Parsons") looked at the profession from a [functionalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structural_functionalism "Structural functionalism") perspective, focusing on medics roles as [experts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expert "Expert"), their altruism, and how they support communities. Other sociologists have taken a [conflict theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conflict_theories "Conflict theories") perspective, looking at how the medical profession secures its own interests. Of these, [Marxist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marxism "Marxism") conflict theory perspective considers how the ruling classes can enact power through medicine, while other theories propose a more [structural pluralist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structural_pluralism "Structural pluralism") approach, exemplified by [Eliot Freidson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliot_Freidson "Eliot Freidson"), looking at how the professions themselves secure influence.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:8-3):291

### Medical education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Medical education")]

The study of [medical education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_education "Medical education") has been a central part of medical sociology since its emergence in the 1950s. The first publication on the topic was Robert Merton's _The Student Physician_. Other scholars who studied the field include [Howard S. Becker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_S._Becker "Howard S. Becker"), with his publication _Boys in White_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:9-6):1

The [hidden curriculum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hidden_curriculum "Hidden curriculum") is a concept in medical education that refers to a distinction between what is officially taught and what is learned by a medical student.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:9-6):16 The concept was introduced by [Philip W. Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_W._Jackson "Philip W. Jackson") in his book _Life in the Classroom_, but developed further by Benson Snyder. The concept has been criticised by Lakomski and there has been considerable debate on the concepts within the educational community.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:9-6):17

### Medical dominance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Medical dominance")]

Writing the 1970s, [Eliot Freidson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliot_Freidson "Eliot Freidson") argued that medicine had reached a point of "professional dominance" over the content of their work, other health professions and their clients by convincing the public of medicine's effectiveness, gaining a legal monopoly over their work, and appropriating other "medical" knowledge through control of training.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:10-7):433 This concept of dominance has been extended to professions as a whole in closure theory, where professions are seen as competing for [scope of practice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scope_of_practice "Scope of practice"), for example in the work of [Andrew Abbott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Abbott_(sociologist) "Andrew Abbott (sociologist)").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:10-7):434 Coburn argues that academic interest in medical dominance has decreased over time due to the increased role of [capitalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitalism "Capitalism") in healthcare in the US,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:10-7):436 challenges to the control of [health policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_policy "Health policy") by [politicians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politician "Politician"), [economists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economist "Economist") and planners, and increased agency of [patients](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patient "Patient") through access to the internet.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:10-7):439 Sociologist nursing professor [Kath M. Melia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kath_M._Melia "Kath M. Melia") argues that so far as nurses are concerned, medical paternalistic attitudes have remained.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-9)

## Medicalization

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Medicalization")]

_[Medicalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicalization "Medicalization")_ describes the process whereby an ever-wider range of human experiences are defined, experienced and treated as a medical condition. Examples of medicalization can be seen in [deviance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deviance_(sociology) "Deviance (sociology)"), such as defining [addiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addiction "Addiction") or [antisocial personality disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisocial_personality_disorder "Antisocial personality disorder") as a medical condition. Feminist scholars have shown that the female body is prone to medicalization, arguing that the tendency of viewing the female body as the [Other](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Other_(philosophy) "Other (philosophy)") has been a factor in this.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:6-10):151

Medicalization can obscure social factors by defining a condition as existing entirely within an individual and can be depoliticizing, suggesting than an intervention should be medical when the best intervention is political. Medicalization can give the profession of medicine undue influence.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:6-10):152

## Social construction of illness

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Social construction of illness")]

See also: [Social construction of disability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_construction_of_disability "Social construction of disability")

Social constructionists study the relationships between ideas about [illness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illness "Illness") and expression, perception and understanding of illness by individuals, institutions and society.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:6-10):148 Social constructionists study why diseases exist in one place and not another, or disappear from a particular area. For example, [premenstrual syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premenstrual_syndrome "Premenstrual syndrome"), [anorexia nervosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anorexia_nervosa "Anorexia nervosa") and [susto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susto "Susto") appear to exist in some cultures but not others.

There are a broad range of social constructionist frameworks used in medical sociology that make different assumptions about the relationships between ideas, social processes and the material world.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:6-10):149 Illnesses vary in the degree to which their definition is socially constructed; some illnesses are straightforwardly biological.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:6-10):150 For straightforwardly biological diseases, it would not be meaningful to describe them as a social construction, though it might be meaningful to study the social processes that resulted in the discovery of the disease.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:6-10):150

Some illnesses are contested when a patient complains about a disease despite the medical community being unable to find a biological mechanism for disease. Examples of contested diseases include [myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myalgic_encephalomyelitis/chronic_fatigue_syndrome "Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome") (ME/CFS), [fibromyalgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibromyalgia "Fibromyalgia") and [Gulf War syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_War_syndrome "Gulf War syndrome"). Contested diseases can be studied as social constructs but there is no biomedical understanding. Some contested diseases, such as ME/CFS, are accepted by the institutions of biomedicine while others, such as [environmental diseases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_disease "Environmental disease"), are not.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:6-10):153

### Sick role

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Sick role")]

The study of the social construction of illness within medical sociology can be traced to [Talcott Parsons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talcott_Parsons "Talcott Parsons")' notion of the [sick role](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sick_role "Sick role").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:6-10):148 Parsons introduced the notion of the sick role in his book _The Social System._[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:1-11):211 Parsons argued that the sick role is a social role approved and enforced by [social norms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_norm "Social norm") and institutional behaviours where an individual is viewed as showing certain behaviour because they are in need of support.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:1-11):212

Parsons argues that defining properties are that the sick person is exempt from normal social roles, that they are not "responsible" for their condition, that they should try to get well, and that they should seek technically competent people to help them.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:1-11):213

The concept of the sick role has been critiqued by sociologists from neo-marxist, phenomonological and social interactionist perspectives, as well as by those with anti-establishment viewpoints.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:2-12):76 Burnham argues that part of this criticism is a rejection of [functionalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Structural_functionalism "Structural functionalism") due to its associations with conservatism. The sick role fell out of favour in the 1990s.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:2-12)

### Labelling theory

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Labelling theory")]

[Labelling theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labeling_theory "Labeling theory") is derived from the work of [Howard S. Becker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_S._Becker "Howard S. Becker"), who studied the sociology of marijuana use. He argued that norms and deviant behaviour are partly the result of the definitions applied by others. [Eliot Freidson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliot_Freidson "Eliot Freidson") applied these concepts to illness.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:1-11):226

Labelling theory separates the aspects of an individual's behaviour caused by an illness, and that which is caused by the application of a label. Freidson distinguished labels based on legitimacy and the degree to which to this legitimacy affected an individual's responsibilities.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:1-11):227

Labelling theory has been criticized on the grounds that it does not explain which behaviours are labelled as deviant and why people engage in behaviours which are labelled as deviant: labelling theory is not a complete theory of deviant behaviour.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:1-11):228

### Mental health

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Mental health")]

An illness framework is the dominant framework for disease in psychiatry and [diagnosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diagnosis "Diagnosis") is considered worthwhile.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:7-13):2 Psychiatry has emphasized the biological when considering mental illness.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:7-13):3 Some psychiatrists have criticized this model: some prefer [biopsychosocial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biopsychosocial_model "Biopsychosocial model") definitions, while others prefer [social constructionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_constructionism "Social constructionism") models, and still others have argued that madness is an intelligent response if all circumstances are understood ([Laing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R.D._Laing "R.D. Laing") and [Esterson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Esterson "Aaron Esterson")). [Thomas Szasz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Szasz "Thomas Szasz"), who trained as a psychiatrist, argued that mental health was a bad concept in his 1961 book _[The Myth of Mental Illness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Myth\_of\_Mental\_Illness "The Myth of Mental Illness")_, arguing that minds can only be ill metaphorically.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:7-13):3

## Doctor–patient relationship

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Doctor–patient relationship")]

The [doctor–patient relationship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor%E2%80%93patient_relationship "Doctor–patient relationship"), the social interactions between healthcare providers and those who interact with them, is studied by medical sociology. There are different models for the interaction between a patient and doctor, which may have been more or less prevalent at different times. One such model is medical consumerism, which has partly given way to [patient consumerism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patient_consumerism?action=edit&redlink=1 "Patient consumerism (page does not exist)").

### Medical paternalism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Medical paternalism")]

[Medical paternalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_paternalism "Medical paternalism") is the perspective that doctors want what is best for the patient and must take decisions on behalf of the patient because the patient is not competent to make their own decisions. Parsons argued that though there was an asymmetry of knowledge and power in the doctor–patient relationship, the medical system provided sufficient safeguards to protect the patient, justifying a paternalistic role by the doctor and medical system.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:3-14):496

A system of medical paternalism was prominent following the second world war through to the mid-1960s. Writing in the 1970s, Eliot Freidson referred to medicine as having "professional dominance", determining its work and defining a conceptualization of the problems that are brought to it and the best solutions to them.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:3-14):497 Professional dominance is defined by three characteristics: practitioners having power over clients, for example through dependency, knowledge, or location asymmetry; control over juniors in the field, requiring juniors' deference and submission; and control over other professions either by excluding them from practice, or placing them under control of the medical profession.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:7-13):161

Yeyoung Oh Nelson argues that this system of paternalism was in part undermined by organizational change in the following decades in the US whereby insurance companies, managers and the pharmaceutical industry started competing for role of conceptualizing and delivering medical services, part of the motive being cost-saving.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:3-14):498

## Bioethics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Bioethics")]

Main article: [Bioethics §Medical sociology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bioethics#Medical_sociology "Bioethics")

[Bioethics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bioethics "Bioethics") studies ethical concern in medical treatment and research. Many scholars believe that bioethics arose due to a perceived lack of accountability of the medical profession, the field has been broadly adopted with most US hospitals offering some form of ethical consultation. The social effects of the field of bioethics have been studied by medical sociologists.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-15):2[Informed consent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Informed_consent#Medical_sociology "Informed consent"), having its roots in bioethics, is the process by which a doctor and a patient agree to a particular intervention. Medical sociology studies the social processes that influence and at times limit consent.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-16)

## Related fields

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Related fields")]

### Social medicine

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Social medicine")]

[Social medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_medicine "Social medicine") is a similar field to medical sociology in that it tries to conceptualize social interactions[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:4-17):241 in investigating how the study of social interactions can be used in medicine.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-18):9 However, the two fields have different training, career paths, titles, funding and publication.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:4-17):241 In the 2010s, Rose and Callard argued that this distinction may be arbitrary.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:4-17):242

In the 1950s, Strauss argued that it was important to maintain the independence of medical sociology from medicine so that there was a different perspective on sociology separate from the aims of medicine.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:4-17):242 Strauss feared that if medical sociology started to adopt the goals expected by medicine it risked losing its focus on analysing society. These fears that have been echoed since by Reid, Gold and Timmermans.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:4-17):248 Rosenfeld argues that the study of sociology focused solely on making recommendations for medicine has limited use for theory building and its findings cease to apply in different social situations.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:4-17):249

Richard Boulton argues that medical sociology and social medicine are "co-produced" in the sense that social medicine responds to the conceptualization of medical practices created by medical sociology and alters medical practice and medical understanding in response, and that the effects of these changes are then analyzed by medical sociology once again.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:4-17):245 He argues that the tendency to view certain theories such as the scientific method ([positivism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positivism "Positivism")) as the basis for all knowledge, and conversely the tendency to view all knowledge as associated with some activity both risk undermining the field of medical sociology.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:4-17):250

### Medical anthropology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Medical_sociology&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Medical anthropology")]

[Peter Conrad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Conrad_(sociologist) "Peter Conrad (sociologist)") notes that [medical anthropology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_anthropology "Medical anthropology") studies some of the same phenomena as medical sociology but argues that medical anthropology has different origins, originally studying medicine within non-western cultures and using different methodologies.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:5-19):91–92 He argues that there was some convergence between the disciplines, as medical sociology started to adopt some of the methodologies of anthropology such as [qualitative research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qualitative_research "Qualitative research") and began to focus more on the patient, and medical anthropology started to focus on western medicine. He argues that more interdisciplinary communication could improve both disciplines.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sociology#cite_note-:5-19):97

**Herbert** "**Harry**" **Stack Sullivan** (February 21, 1892 – January 14, 1949) was an American [neo-Freudian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Freudian "Neo-Freudian")[psychiatrist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychiatrist "Psychiatrist") and [psychoanalyst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychoanalysis "Psychoanalysis") who held that "personality can never be isolated from the complex [interpersonal relationships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interpersonal_relationships "Interpersonal relationships") in which [a] person lives" and that "[t]he field of psychiatry is the field of interpersonal relations under any and all circumstances in which [such] relations exist".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Stack_Sullivan#cite_note-1) Having studied therapists [Sigmund Freud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freud "Freud"), [Adolf Meyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Meyer_(psychiatrist) "Adolf Meyer (psychiatrist)"), and [William Alanson White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Alanson_White "William Alanson White"), he devoted years of clinical and research work to helping people with psychotic illness.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Stack_Sullivan#cite_note-2)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Harry_Stack_Sullivan&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Sullivan was a child of Irish immigrants. He was born and grew up in the then anti-Catholic town of [Norwich, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwich_(city),_New_York "Norwich (city), New York"), resulting in a [social isolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_isolation "Social isolation") that may have inspired his later interest in psychiatry. He attended the Smyrna Union School, then spent two years at [Cornell University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornell_University "Cornell University") from 1909,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Stack_Sullivan#cite_note-3) receiving his medical degree in [Chicago College of Medicine and Surgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_College_of_Medicine_and_Surgery "Chicago College of Medicine and Surgery") in 1917.

## Work

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Harry_Stack_Sullivan&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Work")]

Along with [Clara Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clara_Thompson "Clara Thompson"), [Karen Horney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karen_Horney "Karen Horney"), [Erich Fromm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erich_Fromm "Erich Fromm"), [Otto Allen Will Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Allen_Will_Jr. "Otto Allen Will Jr."), [Erik H. Erikson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erik_H._Erikson "Erik H. Erikson"), and [Frieda Fromm-Reichmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frieda_Fromm-Reichmann "Frieda Fromm-Reichmann"), Sullivan laid the groundwork for understanding the individual based on the network of relationships in which they are enmeshed. He developed a theory of psychiatry based on interpersonal relationships[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Stack_Sullivan#cite_note-4) where cultural forces are largely responsible for [mental illnesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mental_illness "Mental illness")_(see also [social psychiatry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social\_psychiatry "Social psychiatry"))_. In his words, one must pay attention to the "interactional", not the "intrapsychic". This search for satisfaction via personal involvement with others led Sullivan to characterize [loneliness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loneliness "Loneliness") as the most painful human experience. He also extended Freudian psychoanalysis to the treatment of patients with severe mental disorders, particularly [schizophrenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schizophrenia "Schizophrenia").

Besides making the first mention of the [significant other](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Significant_other "Significant other") in psychological literature, Sullivan developed the idea of the "[Self system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self_system "Self system")", a configuration of the personality traits developed in childhood and reinforced by positive affirmation and the security operations developed in childhood to avoid anxiety and threats to self-esteem. Sullivan further defined the Self System as a steering mechanism toward a series of I-You interlocking behaviors—that is, what an individual does is meant to elicit a particular reaction.

Sullivan called these behaviors [Parataxical Integrations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parataxical_Integration "Parataxical Integration") and noted that such action-reaction combinations can become rigid and dominate an adult's thinking pattern, limiting their actions and reactions to the world as the adult sees it, not as it really is. The resulting inaccuracies in judgment Sullivan termed [parataxic distortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parataxic_distortion "Parataxic distortion"), when other persons are perceived or evaluated based on the patterns of previous experience, similar to Freud's notion of [transference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transference "Transference"). Sullivan also introduced the concept of "prototaxic communication" as a more primitive, needy, infantile form of psychic interchange and "syntactic communication" as a mature style of emotional interaction.

Sullivan's work on interpersonal relationships became the foundation of [interpersonal psychoanalysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interpersonal_psychoanalysis "Interpersonal psychoanalysis"), a school of psychoanalytic theory and treatment that stresses detailed exploration of the nuances of patients' patterns of interacting with others.

Sullivan was the first to coin the term "problems in living" to describe the difficulties with self and others that people experience. This phrase was later picked up and popularized by [Thomas Szasz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Szasz "Thomas Szasz"), whose work was a foundational resource for the [antipsychiatry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-psychiatry "Anti-psychiatry") movement. "Problems in living" went on to become the movement's preferred way to refer to the manifestations of mental disturbances.

In 1927, he reviewed the controversial, anonymously published _The Invert and his Social Adjustment_ and in 1929 called it "a remarkable document by a homosexual man of refinement; intended primarily as a guide to the unfortunate sufferers of sexual inversion, and much less open to criticism than anything else of the kind so far published."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Stack_Sullivan#cite_note-5)

He was one of the founders of the [William Alanson White Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Alanson_White_Institute "William Alanson White Institute"), considered by many the world's leading independent psychoanalytic institute, and of the journal _Psychiatry_ in 1937. He headed the [Washington, D.C., School of Psychiatry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C.,_School_of_Psychiatry?action=edit&redlink=1 "Washington, D.C., School of Psychiatry (page does not exist)") from 1936 to 1947.

In 1940, he and colleague [Winfred Overholser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winfred_Overholser "Winfred Overholser"), serving on the [American Psychiatric Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Psychiatric_Association "American Psychiatric Association")'s committee on Military Mobilization, formulated guidelines for the psychological screening of inductees to the U.S. military. He believed, writes one historian, "that sexuality played a minimal role in causing mental disorders and that adult homosexuals should be accepted and left alone."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Stack_Sullivan#cite_note-6) Despite his best efforts, others included homosexuality as a disqualification for military service.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Stack_Sullivan#cite_note-7)

Beginning on December 5, 1940, Sullivan served as psychiatric adviser to [Selective Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selective_Service "Selective Service") director [Clarence A. Dykstra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_A._Dykstra "Clarence A. Dykstra"), but resigned in November 1941 after General [Lewis B. Hershey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Blaine_Hershey "Lewis Blaine Hershey"), who was hostile to psychiatry, became the director.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Stack_Sullivan#cite_note-8) Sullivan then took part in establishing the [Office of War Information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_War_Information "Office of War Information") in 1942.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Stack_Sullivan#cite_note-9)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Harry_Stack_Sullivan&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Sullivan spent the last 22 years of his life in a relationship with James Inscoe, who was 20 years younger than Sullivan.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Stack_Sullivan#cite_note-10) Although some contemporaries and historians have regarded Inscoe as an adopted son, the biography of his colleague Helen Swick Perry mentions the relationship, suggesting that close friends were aware they were partners.

Sullivan died in Paris in 1949.

## Writings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Harry_Stack_Sullivan&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Writings")]

Although Sullivan published little in his lifetime, he influenced generations of mental health professionals, especially through his lectures at [Chestnut Lodge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chestnut_Lodge "Chestnut Lodge") in [Rockville, Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockville,_Maryland "Rockville, Maryland"). [Leston Havens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leston_Havens "Leston Havens") called him the most important underground influence in American psychoanalysis. His ideas were collected and published posthumously, edited by Helen Swick Perry, who also published a detailed biography in 1982 (Perry, 1982, _Psychiatrist of America_).

## Works

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Harry_Stack_Sullivan&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Works")]

The following works are in Special Collections (MSA SC 5547) at the [Maryland State Archives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland_State_Archives "Maryland State Archives") in Annapolis: Conceptions of Modern Psychiatry, Soundscriber Transcriptions (Feb. 1945-May 1945); Lectures 1-97 (begins Oct. 2, 1942); Georgetown University Medical School Lectures (1939); Personal Psychopathology (1929–1933); The Psychiatry of Character and its Deviations-undated notes.

His writings include:

1.   _The Interpersonal Theory of Psychiatry_ (1953)
2.   "The Psychiatric Interview" (1954)
3.   _Conceptions of Modern Psychiatry_ (1947/1966)

## Relationship to the Sullivanians

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Harry_Stack_Sullivan&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Relationship to the Sullivanians")]

After Sullivan's death, [Saul B. Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saul_B._Newton "Saul B. Newton") and his wife Jane Pearce established the Sullivan Institute for Research in Psychoanalysis in New York City, whose therapists and patients were commonly known as "Sullivanians".

Newton and Pearce had worked with Sullivan at the William Alanson White Institute, and Pearce was a psychiatrist who studied with Sullivan in the late 1940s.

Although the institute was named for Sullivan, it is widely regarded as a [cult](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult "Cult"), offering a distorted view of Sullivan's teachings.
