**Herbert** "**Harry**" **Stack Sullivan** (February 21, 1892 – January 14, 1949) was an American [neo-Freudian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Freudian "Neo-Freudian")[psychiatrist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychiatrist "Psychiatrist") and [psychoanalyst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychoanalysis "Psychoanalysis") who held that "personality can never be isolated from the complex [interpersonal relationships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interpersonal_relationships "Interpersonal relationships") in which [a] person lives" and that "[t]he field of psychiatry is the field of interpersonal relations under any and all circumstances in which [such] relations exist".[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Stack_Sullivan#cite_note-1) Having studied therapists [Sigmund Freud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freud "Freud"), [Adolf Meyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adolf_Meyer_(psychiatrist) "Adolf Meyer (psychiatrist)"), and [William Alanson White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Alanson_White "William Alanson White"), he devoted years of clinical and research work to helping people with psychotic illness.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Stack_Sullivan#cite_note-2)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Harry_Stack_Sullivan&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Sullivan was a child of Irish immigrants. He was born and grew up in the then anti-Catholic town of [Norwich, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwich_(city),_New_York "Norwich (city), New York"), resulting in a [social isolation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_isolation "Social isolation") that may have inspired his later interest in psychiatry. He attended the Smyrna Union School, then spent two years at [Cornell University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornell_University "Cornell University") from 1909,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Stack_Sullivan#cite_note-3) receiving his medical degree in [Chicago College of Medicine and Surgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_College_of_Medicine_and_Surgery "Chicago College of Medicine and Surgery") in 1917.

## Work

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Harry_Stack_Sullivan&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Work")]

Along with [Clara Thompson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clara_Thompson "Clara Thompson"), [Karen Horney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karen_Horney "Karen Horney"), [Erich Fromm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erich_Fromm "Erich Fromm"), [Otto Allen Will Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Allen_Will_Jr. "Otto Allen Will Jr."), [Erik H. Erikson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erik_H._Erikson "Erik H. Erikson"), and [Frieda Fromm-Reichmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frieda_Fromm-Reichmann "Frieda Fromm-Reichmann"), Sullivan laid the groundwork for understanding the individual based on the network of relationships in which they are enmeshed. He developed a theory of psychiatry based on interpersonal relationships[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Stack_Sullivan#cite_note-4) where cultural forces are largely responsible for [mental illnesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mental_illness "Mental illness")_(see also [social psychiatry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social\_psychiatry "Social psychiatry"))_. In his words, one must pay attention to the "interactional", not the "intrapsychic". This search for satisfaction via personal involvement with others led Sullivan to characterize [loneliness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loneliness "Loneliness") as the most painful human experience. He also extended Freudian psychoanalysis to the treatment of patients with severe mental disorders, particularly [schizophrenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schizophrenia "Schizophrenia").

Besides making the first mention of the [significant other](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Significant_other "Significant other") in psychological literature, Sullivan developed the idea of the "[Self system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self_system "Self system")", a configuration of the personality traits developed in childhood and reinforced by positive affirmation and the security operations developed in childhood to avoid anxiety and threats to self-esteem. Sullivan further defined the Self System as a steering mechanism toward a series of I-You interlocking behaviors—that is, what an individual does is meant to elicit a particular reaction.

Sullivan called these behaviors [Parataxical Integrations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parataxical_Integration "Parataxical Integration") and noted that such action-reaction combinations can become rigid and dominate an adult's thinking pattern, limiting their actions and reactions to the world as the adult sees it, not as it really is. The resulting inaccuracies in judgment Sullivan termed [parataxic distortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parataxic_distortion "Parataxic distortion"), when other persons are perceived or evaluated based on the patterns of previous experience, similar to Freud's notion of [transference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transference "Transference"). Sullivan also introduced the concept of "prototaxic communication" as a more primitive, needy, infantile form of psychic interchange and "syntactic communication" as a mature style of emotional interaction.

Sullivan's work on interpersonal relationships became the foundation of [interpersonal psychoanalysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interpersonal_psychoanalysis "Interpersonal psychoanalysis"), a school of psychoanalytic theory and treatment that stresses detailed exploration of the nuances of patients' patterns of interacting with others.

Sullivan was the first to coin the term "problems in living" to describe the difficulties with self and others that people experience. This phrase was later picked up and popularized by [Thomas Szasz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Szasz "Thomas Szasz"), whose work was a foundational resource for the [antipsychiatry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-psychiatry "Anti-psychiatry") movement. "Problems in living" went on to become the movement's preferred way to refer to the manifestations of mental disturbances.

In 1927, he reviewed the controversial, anonymously published _The Invert and his Social Adjustment_ and in 1929 called it "a remarkable document by a homosexual man of refinement; intended primarily as a guide to the unfortunate sufferers of sexual inversion, and much less open to criticism than anything else of the kind so far published."[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Stack_Sullivan#cite_note-5)

He was one of the founders of the [William Alanson White Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Alanson_White_Institute "William Alanson White Institute"), considered by many the world's leading independent psychoanalytic institute, and of the journal _Psychiatry_ in 1937. He headed the [Washington, D.C., School of Psychiatry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C.,_School_of_Psychiatry?action=edit&redlink=1 "Washington, D.C., School of Psychiatry (page does not exist)") from 1936 to 1947.

In 1940, he and colleague [Winfred Overholser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winfred_Overholser "Winfred Overholser"), serving on the [American Psychiatric Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Psychiatric_Association "American Psychiatric Association")'s committee on Military Mobilization, formulated guidelines for the psychological screening of inductees to the U.S. military. He believed, writes one historian, "that sexuality played a minimal role in causing mental disorders and that adult homosexuals should be accepted and left alone."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Stack_Sullivan#cite_note-6) Despite his best efforts, others included homosexuality as a disqualification for military service.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Stack_Sullivan#cite_note-7)

Beginning on December 5, 1940, Sullivan served as psychiatric adviser to [Selective Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selective_Service "Selective Service") director [Clarence A. Dykstra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarence_A._Dykstra "Clarence A. Dykstra"), but resigned in November 1941 after General [Lewis B. Hershey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lewis_Blaine_Hershey "Lewis Blaine Hershey"), who was hostile to psychiatry, became the director.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Stack_Sullivan#cite_note-8) Sullivan then took part in establishing the [Office of War Information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_War_Information "Office of War Information") in 1942.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Stack_Sullivan#cite_note-9)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Harry_Stack_Sullivan&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Sullivan spent the last 22 years of his life in a relationship with James Inscoe, who was 20 years younger than Sullivan.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Stack_Sullivan#cite_note-10) Although some contemporaries and historians have regarded Inscoe as an adopted son, the biography of his colleague Helen Swick Perry mentions the relationship, suggesting that close friends were aware they were partners.

Sullivan died in Paris in 1949.

## Writings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Harry_Stack_Sullivan&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Writings")]

Although Sullivan published little in his lifetime, he influenced generations of mental health professionals, especially through his lectures at [Chestnut Lodge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chestnut_Lodge "Chestnut Lodge") in [Rockville, Maryland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockville,_Maryland "Rockville, Maryland"). [Leston Havens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leston_Havens "Leston Havens") called him the most important underground influence in American psychoanalysis. His ideas were collected and published posthumously, edited by Helen Swick Perry, who also published a detailed biography in 1982 (Perry, 1982, _Psychiatrist of America_).

## Works

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Harry_Stack_Sullivan&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Works")]

The following works are in Special Collections (MSA SC 5547) at the [Maryland State Archives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maryland_State_Archives "Maryland State Archives") in Annapolis: Conceptions of Modern Psychiatry, Soundscriber Transcriptions (Feb. 1945-May 1945); Lectures 1-97 (begins Oct. 2, 1942); Georgetown University Medical School Lectures (1939); Personal Psychopathology (1929–1933); The Psychiatry of Character and its Deviations-undated notes.

His writings include:

1.   _The Interpersonal Theory of Psychiatry_ (1953)
2.   "The Psychiatric Interview" (1954)
3.   _Conceptions of Modern Psychiatry_ (1947/1966)
4.   _Schizophrenia as a Human Process_ (1962)

## Relationship to the Sullivanians

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Harry_Stack_Sullivan&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Relationship to the Sullivanians")]

After Sullivan's death, [Saul B. Newton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saul_B._Newton "Saul B. Newton") and his wife Jane Pearce established the Sullivan Institute for Research in Psychoanalysis in New York City, whose therapists and patients were commonly known as "Sullivanians".

Newton and Pearce had worked with Sullivan at the William Alanson White Institute, and Pearce was a psychiatrist who studied with Sullivan in the late 1940s.

Although the institute was named for Sullivan, it is widely regarded as a [cult](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult "Cult"), offering a distorted view of Sullivan's teachings.

# Montreal-born doctor gets posthumous Nobel honour

Montreal-born scientist Dr. Ralph Steinman will be awarded the Nobel Prize for Medicine, despite his death three days earlier.

## Nobel committee had been unaware of recipient's recent death

CBC News · Posted: Oct 03, 2011 5:54 AM EDT | Last Updated: October 4, 2011

![Image 2: Text to Speech Icon](https://www.cbc.ca/a/assets/texttospeech.svg)

Listen to this article

Estimated 3 minutes

The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

## Social Sharing

Montreal-born scientist Dr. Ralph Steinman will be awarded the Nobel Prize for Medicine, despite his death three days earlier.

Steinman and two other scientists were announced as winners of the Nobel in medicine on Monday.

"The events that have occurred are unique and, to the best of our knowledge, are unprecedented in the history of the Nobel Prize," the Nobel Foundation said in a statement.

"According to the statutes of the Nobel Foundation, work produced by a person since deceased shall not be given an award. However, the statutes specify that if a person has been awarded a prize and has died before receiving it, the prize may be presented."

The committee said the decision to give the award to Steinman was made in good faith under the assumption that he was alive, and compared the situation to someone who was named as a laureate but died before the actual Nobel Prize award ceremony.

Steinman was honoured for "his discovery of the dendritic cell and its role in adaptive immunity."

Steinman's family described it as a bittersweet day. His daughter, Alexis Steinman, said while part of him would likely have been humbled by the Nobel, it probably would have "knocked his socks off."

![Image 3](https://i.cbc.ca/ais/1.2044064,1381648375000/full/max/0/default.jpg?im=Crop%2Crect%3D%280%2C0%2C1180%2C1669%29%3B)

The late Ralph M. Steinman was cited by the Nobel committee for his 'discovery of the dendritic cell and its role in adaptive immunity,' which start and regulate the body's immune response. ((Rockefeller University Press/Nobel Prize.org))

### Arming immune system

Canadian Dr. Alan Bernstein, who heads the Global HIV Vaccine Enterprise in New York, met Steinman about 3 ½ years ago.

Bernstein described Steinman as a very warm,generous and determined individual who was commited to pushing his science.

Steinman realized the dendritic cells could potentially arm the immune system against incoming pathogens such as bacteria and viruses, and perhaps against cancer, Bernstein said.

"He was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer four years ago," Rockefeller University in New York, said in a statement.

Steinman, 68, recently moved into a modern lab at the university's Center for Immunology and Immune Diseases, where he was using dendritic cells to fight the pancreatic cancer.

![Image 4](https://i.cbc.ca/ais/1.2044063,1381648375000/full/max/0/default.jpg?im=Crop%2Crect%3D%280%2C0%2C1180%2C665%29%3B)

Bruce Beutler, left, and Jules Hoffmann, right, received the Balzan Prize in Bern, Switzerland, in 2007. Beutler and Hoffmann were cited by the Nobel committee for their discoveries concerning the activation of innate immunity. ((Lukas Lehmann/Keystone/Associated Press))

It's impossible to say whether Steinman lived longer thanks to the cells, but he did live longer than average for someone with pancreatic cancer, Bernstein noted.

Steinman shared the award with American Bruce Beutler and French scientist Jules Hoffmann, the Nobel committee at Stockholm's Karolinska institute said.

Steinman's $1.5 million US prize will be given to his estate. His daughter said he always gave prize money to a foundation to help aspiring scientists and they plan to do the same.

The medicine award kicked off a week of Nobel Prize announcements, and will be followed by the physics prize on Tuesday, chemistry on Wednesday, literature on Thursday and the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday. The winners of the economics award will be announced on Oct. 10.

The coveted prizes were established by wealthy Swedish industrialist Alfred Nobel—the inventor of dynamite—except for the economics award, which was created by Sweden's central bank in 1968 in Nobel's memory. The prizes are always handed out on Dec. 10, on the anniversary of Nobel's death in 1896.

Last year's medicine award went to British professor Robert Edwards [for fertility research](http://www.cbc.ca/news/technology/story/2010/10/04/nobel-prize-medical.html)that led to the first test tube baby.

# Montreal-born doctor gets posthumous Nobel honour

Montreal-born scientist Dr. Ralph Steinman will be awarded the Nobel Prize for Medicine, despite his death three days earlier.

## Nobel committee had been unaware of recipient's recent death

CBC News · Posted: Oct 03, 2011 5:54 AM EDT | Last Updated: October 4, 2011

![Image 2: Text to Speech Icon](https://www.cbc.ca/a/assets/texttospeech.svg)

Listen to this article

Estimated 3 minutes

## Social Sharing

Montreal-born scientist Dr. Ralph Steinman will be awarded the Nobel Prize for Medicine, despite his death three days earlier.

Steinman and two other scientists were announced as winners of the Nobel in medicine on Monday.

"The events that have occurred are unique and, to the best of our knowledge, are unprecedented in the history of the Nobel Prize," the Nobel Foundation said in a statement.

"According to the statutes of the Nobel Foundation, work produced by a person since deceased shall not be given an award. However, the statutes specify that if a person has been awarded a prize and has died before receiving it, the prize may be presented."

The committee said the decision to give the award to Steinman was made in good faith under the assumption that he was alive, and compared the situation to someone who was named as a laureate but died before the actual Nobel Prize award ceremony.

Steinman was honoured for "his discovery of the dendritic cell and its role in adaptive immunity."

Steinman's family described it as a bittersweet day. His daughter, Alexis Steinman, said while part of him would likely have been humbled by the Nobel, it probably would have "knocked his socks off."

![Image 3](https://i.cbc.ca/ais/1.2044064,1381648375000/full/max/0/default.jpg?im=Crop%2Crect%3D%280%2C0%2C1180%2C1669%29%3B)

The late Ralph M. Steinman was cited by the Nobel committee for his 'discovery of the dendritic cell and its role in adaptive immunity,' which start and regulate the body's immune response. ((Rockefeller University Press/Nobel Prize.org))

### Arming immune system

Canadian Dr. Alan Bernstein, who heads the Global HIV Vaccine Enterprise in New York, met Steinman about 3 ½ years ago.

Bernstein described Steinman as a very warm,generous and determined individual who was commited to pushing his science.

Steinman realized the dendritic cells could potentially arm the immune system against incoming pathogens such as bacteria and viruses, and perhaps against cancer, Bernstein said.

"He was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer four years ago," Rockefeller University in New York, said in a statement.

Steinman, 68, recently moved into a modern lab at the university's Center for Immunology and Immune Diseases, where he was using dendritic cells to fight the pancreatic cancer.

![Image 4](https://i.cbc.ca/ais/1.2044063,1381648375000/full/max/0/default.jpg?im=Crop%2Crect%3D%280%2C0%2C1180%2C665%29%3B)

Bruce Beutler, left, and Jules Hoffmann, right, received the Balzan Prize in Bern, Switzerland, in 2007. Beutler and Hoffmann were cited by the Nobel committee for their discoveries concerning the activation of innate immunity. ((Lukas Lehmann/Keystone/Associated Press))

It's impossible to say whether Steinman lived longer thanks to the cells, but he did live longer than average for someone with pancreatic cancer, Bernstein noted.

Steinman shared the award with American Bruce Beutler and French scientist Jules Hoffmann, the Nobel committee at Stockholm's Karolinska institute said.

Steinman's $1.5 million US prize will be given to his estate. His daughter said he always gave prize money to a foundation to help aspiring scientists and they plan to do the same.

The medicine award kicked off a week of Nobel Prize announcements, and will be followed by the physics prize on Tuesday, chemistry on Wednesday, literature on Thursday and the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday. The winners of the economics award will be announced on Oct. 10.

The coveted prizes were established by wealthy Swedish industrialist Alfred Nobel—the inventor of dynamite—except for the economics award, which was created by Sweden's central bank in 1968 in Nobel's memory. The prizes are always handed out on Dec. 10, on the anniversary of Nobel's death in 1896.

Last year's medicine award went to British professor Robert Edwards [for fertility research](http://www.cbc.ca/news/technology/story/2010/10/04/nobel-prize-medical.html)that led to the first test tube baby.

messages.content:
Reasoning: medium
Read pages for a research assistant and follow useful links recursively. During
extraction, only the supplied page is evidence. The question defines what to look
for; parent reasoning guides navigation but is not this page's evidence.
Extraction uses the original question and current page, not the search query or
parent's hypothesis. Keep facts relevant to any part of the original question.
During navigation, a supplied local relation is a task, not evidence. Follow links
that establish or contradict it. Return when it is settled or has no useful route
here; other unresolved relations belong to the parent. Do not solve the whole
question again inside every branch.

Preserve exact relevant names and rows with their headers, values, units, dates
and scope. Never replace relevant rows with ellipses, examples or instructions to
continue the list. If all rows cannot fit, prioritize rows useful to the question
and explicitly mark omissions. A partial, restricted or truncated list is not the
complete candidate set. Missing fields are unknown. Keep relevant discoveries even
if they answer a different part of the original question.

Follow links likely to fill a candidate's missing condition or reach the required
document/year. An index is useful when it offers a concrete route to the needed
record; generic menus or keyword collections alone do not justify expansion.
Link-menu rank is only a hint: check the destination's subject and scope. If content
repeats, try a detail page or another supported route. Links outside the menu and inferred
paths on an observed site are allowed. Child notes are returned automatically;
do not copy their facts into your own note. Retain useful unvisited links even
when expansion stops.

For extraction return:
**Final Information**
**Page:** Actual title and URL.
**Evidence:** Exact relevant facts/rows and short supporting quotes.
**Connections:** Candidate and identifying relation supported or contradicted here; label deductions.
**Coverage:** Actual entities, years, population; full list, subset or excerpt.
**Missing:** Requested fields this page does not establish.
**Next links:** One URL and missing relation per line, most useful first. With Expand yes,
the first eligible route is executed without another selection call, within the budget.
**Expand:** yes or no, and why.
**Status:** partial
Use answered only if this page supplies all requested facts, partial for useful
incomplete evidence, or not_found with a brief reason. During navigation, call

# The man behind the prize – Alfred Nobel

## For the greatest benefit to humankind

Alfred Nobel was an inventor, entrepreneur, scientist and businessman who also wrote poetry and drama. His varied interests are reflected in the prize he established and which he lay the foundation for in 1895 when he wrote his last will, leaving much of his wealth to the establishment of the prize.

Since 1901, the Nobel Prize has been honouring men and women from around the world for outstanding achievements in physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature and for work in peace.

## Quick facts

*   Born: 21 October 1833
*   Died: 10 December 1896
*   Known for: inventing dynamite and holder of 355 patents
*   Professions: chemist, inventor, engineer, entrepreneur, businessman, author
*   Will: left 31 million Swedish kronor (SEK) to fund the prizes

### [The last will and testament](https://www.nobelprize.org/alfred-nobel/alfred-nobels-will/)

Alfred Nobel signed his last will in Paris on 27 November 1895. He specified that the bulk of his fortune should be divided into five parts and to be used for prizes in physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature and peace to “those who, during the preceding year, shall have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind.”

[![Image 2: Alfred Nobel's poem The Riddle](blob:http://localhost/aef335eb562a1da6957ce25a574b4aa1)](https://www.nobelprize.org/alfred-nobel/alfred-nobels-will/)

The will of Alfred Nobel.

© Nobel Media. Photo: Alexander Mahmoud

### Key events in Alfred Nobel’s life

1.   1833 Alfred Nobel is born in Stockholm, Sweden. In the same year, his father, Immanuel Nobel, goes bankrupt. 
2.   1838 Immanuel Nobel arrives in St Petersburg, Russia, where he starts a mechanical workshop; he leaves his family behind in Sweden. He lands a contract with a Russian general, who is interested in the Swedish inventor’s designs for sea and land mines. His business flourishes and evolves to a large mechanical engineering company. 
3.   1842 The Nobel family is reunited in St Petersburg, Russia. 
4.   1850 – 1852 At the age of 17, Alfred Nobel speaks five languages fluently. He travels to Paris and works for one year in the laboratory of T. Jules Pelouze. He also travels to Italy, Germany and the United States (US). 
5.   1853 – 1856 Immanuel Nobel’s company goes bankrupt as the Crimean War ends and the Russian military cancel orders. Alfred Nobel searches desperately for new products. Nikolai N. Zinin, Nobel’s chemistry teacher, reminds him of nitroglycerin. 
6.   1862 Alfred Nobel starts his experiments with nitroglycerin. 
7.   1863 Alfred Nobel moves back to Stockholm and obtains the first patent on nitroglycerin (blasting oil) as an industrial explosive. 
8.   1864 Alfred Nobel patents a detonator (blasting cap) for triggering the explosion of nitroglycerin and forms the company Nitroglycerin AB. Emil, Alfred Nobel’s brother, is killed during the preparation of nitroglycerin at Heleneborg, Stockholm. 
9.   1865 Alfred Nobel improves the blasting cap design and moves to Germany to set up the Alfred Nobel & Co Factory in Krümmel near Hamburg. 
10.   1866 A violent explosion destroys the Krümmel plant in Germany. Experimenting on a raft anchored on the river Elbe, Alfred Nobel tries to make nitroglycerin safer to handle. He finds that nitroglycerin is stabilised by the addition of kieselguhr (a siliceous deposit; also known as diatomaceous earth) and calls this mixture dynamite. (From Greek _dynamis_ meaning “power”).

He also establishes the United States Blasting Oil Company in the US. 
11.   1867 Alfred Nobel obtains a patent for dynamite in Sweden. 
12.   1871 Alfred Nobel establishes the British Dynamite Company (Ardeer, Scotland, UK). In 1877 the company name is changed to Nobel’s Explosives Company. 
13.   1872 Immanuel, Alfred Nobel’s father, passes away. 
14.   1873 At the age of 40 Alfred Nobel is a wealthy man. He moves to Paris and settles at Avenue Malakoff.

The manufacture of nitroglycerin and dynamite starts at Ardeer, Scotland, UK. 
15.   1875 Alfred Nobel invents blasting gelatine in Paris and establishes Société Générale pour la Fabrication de la Dynamite in Paris. 
16.   1876 Alfred Nobel obtains a patent on blasting gelatine.

Dynamitaktiengesellschaft (DAG), formerly Alfred Nobel & Co (Hamburg, Germany), is formed.

Alfred Nobel advertises for a housekeeper/personal secretary, meets with Bertha Kinsky von Chinic und Tettau (later von Suttner) and hires her. She leaves her employment after a short time and becomes a leading peace activist. 
17.   1880 Dynamite Nobel is formed by merging Nobel’s Italian and Swiss companies. 
18.   1881 Alfred Nobel buys an estate and laboratory at Sevran outside Paris. 
19.   1885 German Union is formed by merging Dynamitaktiengesellschaft (DAG) and a group of German dynamite companies. 
20.   1886 Nobel-Dynamite Trust Co (London, UK) is formed by merging Dynamitaktiengesellschaft (DAG) and the Nobel’s Explosives Company. 
21.   1887 Nobel obtains a patent for the blasting powder “ballistite” in France. 
22.   1889 Andriette, Alfred Nobel’s mother, passes away. 
23.   1891 Alfred Nobel leaves Paris and settles in Sanremo, Italy, after a dispute with the French government over ballistite. 
24.   1893 Alfred Nobel hires the young engineer Ragnar Sohlman, who he later names executor of his will and testament. 
25.   1894 Alfred Nobel buys a small machine works (Bofors-Gullspång) and a manor (Björkborn) at Karlskoga, Sweden. 
26.   1895 The third and final will of Alfred Nobel is signed at the Swedish-Norwegian Club in Paris. 
27.   1896 Alfred Nobel dies, at the age of 63, in his home in Sanremo, Italy, on 10 December 1896. 
28.   1901 The first Nobel Prizes are awarded on 10 December.

# The man behind the prize – Alfred Nobel

## For the greatest benefit to humankind

Alfred Nobel was an inventor, entrepreneur, scientist and businessman who also wrote poetry and drama. His varied interests are reflected in the prize he established and which he lay the foundation for in 1895 when he wrote his last will, leaving much of his wealth to the establishment of the prize.

Since 1901, the Nobel Prize has been honouring men and women from around the world for outstanding achievements in physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature and for work in peace.

## Quick facts

*   Born: 21 October 1833
*   Died: 10 December 1896
*   Known for: inventing dynamite and holder of 355 patents
*   Professions: chemist, inventor, engineer, entrepreneur, businessman, author
*   Will: left 31 million Swedish kronor (SEK) to fund the prizes

### [The last will and testament](https://www.nobelprize.org/alfred-nobel/alfred-nobels-will/)

Alfred Nobel signed his last will in Paris on 27 November 1895. He specified that the bulk of his fortune should be divided into five parts and to be used for prizes in physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature and peace to “those who, during the preceding year, shall have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind.”

[![Image 2: Alfred Nobel's poem The Riddle](blob:http://localhost/aef335eb562a1da6957ce25a574b4aa1)](https://www.nobelprize.org/alfred-nobel/alfred-nobels-will/)

The will of Alfred Nobel.

© Nobel Media. Photo: Alexander Mahmoud

### Key events in Alfred Nobel’s life

1.   1833 Alfred Nobel is born in Stockholm, Sweden. In the same year, his father, Immanuel Nobel, goes bankrupt. 
2.   1838 Immanuel Nobel arrives in St Petersburg, Russia, where he starts a mechanical workshop; he leaves his family behind in Sweden. He lands a contract with a Russian general, who is interested in the Swedish inventor’s designs for sea and land mines. His business flourishes and evolves to a large mechanical engineering company. 
3.   1842 The Nobel family is reunited in St Petersburg, Russia. 
4.   1850 – 1852 At the age of 17, Alfred Nobel speaks five languages fluently. He travels to Paris and works for one year in the laboratory of T. Jules Pelouze. He also travels to Italy, Germany and the United States (US). 
5.   1853 – 1856 Immanuel Nobel’s company goes bankrupt as the Crimean War ends and the Russian military cancel orders. Alfred Nobel searches desperately for new products. Nikolai N. Zinin, Nobel’s chemistry teacher, reminds him of nitroglycerin. 
6.   1862 Alfred Nobel starts his experiments with nitroglycerin. 
7.   1863 Alfred Nobel moves back to Stockholm and obtains the first patent on nitroglycerin (blasting oil) as an industrial explosive. 
8.   1864 Alfred Nobel patents a detonator (blasting cap) for triggering the explosion of nitroglycerin and forms the company Nitroglycerin AB. Emil, Alfred Nobel’s brother, is killed during the preparation of nitroglycerin at Heleneborg, Stockholm. 
9.   1865 Alfred Nobel improves the blasting cap design and moves to Germany to set up the Alfred Nobel & Co Factory in Krümmel near Hamburg. 
10.   1866 A violent explosion destroys the Krümmel plant in Germany. Experimenting on a raft anchored on the river Elbe, Alfred Nobel tries to make nitroglycerin safer to handle. He finds that nitroglycerin is stabilised by the addition of kieselguhr (a siliceous deposit; also known as diatomaceous earth) and calls this mixture dynamite. (From Greek _dynamis_ meaning “power”).

He also establishes the United States Blasting Oil Company in the US. 
11.   1867 Alfred Nobel obtains a patent for dynamite in Sweden. 
12.   1871 Alfred Nobel establishes the British Dynamite Company (Ardeer, Scotland, UK). In 1877 the company name is changed to Nobel’s Explosives Company. 
13.   1872 Immanuel, Alfred Nobel’s father, passes away. 
14.   1873 At the age of 40 Alfred Nobel is a wealthy man. He moves to Paris and settles at Avenue Malakoff.

The manufacture of nitroglycerin and dynamite starts at Ardeer, Scotland, UK. 
15.   1875 Alfred Nobel invents blasting gelatine in Paris and establishes Société Générale pour la Fabrication de la Dynamite in Paris. 
16.   1876 Alfred Nobel obtains a patent on blasting gelatine.

Dynamitaktiengesellschaft (DAG), formerly Alfred Nobel & Co (Hamburg, Germany), is formed.

Alfred Nobel advertises for a housekeeper/personal secretary, meets with Bertha Kinsky von Chinic und Tettau (later von Suttner) and hires her. She leaves her employment after a short time and becomes a leading peace activist. 
17.   1880 Dynamite Nobel is formed by merging Nobel’s Italian and Swiss companies. 
18.   1881 Alfred Nobel buys an estate and laboratory at Sevran outside Paris. 
19.   1885 German Union is formed by merging Dynamitaktiengesellschaft (DAG) and a group of German dynamite companies. 
20.   1886 Nobel-Dynamite Trust Co (London, UK) is formed by merging Dynamitaktiengesellschaft (DAG) and the Nobel’s Explosives Company. 
21.   1887 Nobel obtains a patent for the blasting powder “ballistite” in France. 
22.   1889 Andriette, Alfred Nobel’s mother, passes away. 
23.   1891 Alfred Nobel leaves Paris and settles in Sanremo, Italy, after a dispute with the French government over ballistite. 
24.   1893 Alfred Nobel hires the young engineer Ragnar Sohlman, who he later names executor of his will and testament. 
25.   1894 Alfred Nobel buys a small machine works (Bofors-Gullspång) and a manor (Björkborn) at Karlskoga, Sweden. 
26.   1895 The third and final will of Alfred Nobel is signed at the Swedish-Norwegian Club in Paris. 
27.   1896 Alfred Nobel dies, at the age of 63, in his home in Sanremo, Italy, on 10 December 1896. 
28.   1901 The first Nobel Prizes are awarded on 10 December.

[More about the Nobel Prize-awarding institutions](https://www.nobelprize.org/the-nobel-prize-organisation/prize-awarding-institutions/)

## Quick facts

*   The nomination processes start in September each year.
*   No person can nominate herself/himself for a Nobel Prize.
*   The names of the nominees cannot be revealed until 50 years later.

## The nomination process

### Nomination starts

The Nobel Peace Prize has frequently caused controversy. # Nomination archive

![Image 1: Notes from the Norwegian Nobel Committee Archives](https://www.nobelprize.org/nomination/archive/nomination-king-1.jpg)  
From the archives. Courtesy of the Norwegian Nobel Committee.

Nominations for the Nobel Prizes are handled by the Nobel Prize awarding institutions. Here, all nominations are collected in one database. Explore and search the nomination database!

[More about the Nobel Prize awarding institutions](https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_organizations/prize_awarders/)

## The nomination database

The database is not complete. Names of the nominees and other information about the nominations cannot be revealed until 50 years later. Due to internal work processes there is also at times a delay until a new year of data is available. Note that for the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, only data until 1953 is currently available. The table below summarizes the currect status. See the [manual](https://www.nobelprize.org/nomination/archive/manual.php) for more details.

Number of nominations in chemistry from 1901 to 1975:4249
Number of nominations in physiology or medicine from 1901 to 1953:5110
Number of nominations in literature from 1901 to 1975:4533
Number of nominations in peace from 1901 to 1975:5230
Total:23141

# Nomination archive

![Image 1: Notes from the Norwegian Nobel Committee Archives](https://www.nobelprize.org/nomination/archive/nomination-king-1.jpg)  
From the archives. Courtesy of the Norwegian Nobel Committee.

Nominations for the Nobel Prizes are handled by the Nobel Prize awarding institutions. Here, all nominations are collected in one database. Explore and search the nomination database!

[More about the Nobel Prize awarding institutions](https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_organizations/prize_awarders/)

## The nomination database

The database is not complete. Names of the nominees and other information about the nominations cannot be revealed until 50 years later. Due to internal work processes there is also at times a delay until a new year of data is available. Note that for the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, only data until 1953 is currently available. The table below summarizes the currect status. See the [manual](https://www.nobelprize.org/nomination/archive/manual.php) for more details.

Number of nominations in chemistry from 1901 to 1975:4249
Number of nominations in physiology or medicine from 1901 to 1953:5110
Number of nominations in literature from 1901 to 1975:4533
Number of nominations in peace from 1901 to 1975:5230
Total:23141

# All Nobel Prizes

Between 1901 and 2025, the Nobel Prizes and the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel were awarded 633 times to 1,026 people and organisations. With some receiving the Nobel Prize more than once, this makes a total of 990 individuals and 28 organisations. Below, you can view the full list of Nobel Prizes and Nobel Prize laureates.
