 Another long article in the Times, this time about “Europe”, continent? Union? Concept? History?  
[http://opinionator.blogs.nytimes.com/2012/01/09/where-is-europe/?nl=opinion&emc=tya1](http://opinionator.blogs.nytimes.com/2012/01/09/where-is-europe/?nl=opinion&emc=tya1)     
*   Subhash— January 10, 2012 at 9:05 pm Let us get back to the original chart of Nobel prizes. I noticed that before 1940 Germany was the dominant Nobel country. It also was the country with a long history -since the 1880s- of providing health and retirement insurance to its citizens. Britain too had a sort of health insurance system but not as well developed as Germany. After WW II the British system became gradually more widespread. Britain also shows larger numbers of Nobel prizes in the post WW II period until the late 1970s. In the US, the Social Security and Medicare act was passed in 1965. The US Nobel numbers also went up impressively. Do I see some correlation between general welfare of the population and the number of Nobel prizes here?     
    *   guedy— January 10, 2012 at 9:16 pm Do you really? If I follow your logic, when Germany developed more health and retirement benefits, it had more Nobel Prizes; when the UK did after WWII, it had more Nobel Prizes. When the US….  
 Just a sec: the Social Security act was passed in 1935, not 1965. Medicare was added in 1965 to make the State systems more coordinated at the Federal level.  
 But if you want to establish a correlation between Social programs and Nobel Prizes, then that logic must be flawed: why is it that as Germany and Britain dramatically increased their social programs post-WWII, their numbers of Nobel Laureates diminished?  
 I hesitate to bring up this point, but do you really want to credit pre-WWII National Socialism in Germany for both being a model of social responsibility AND a breeding ground for Nobel Prizes?     
        *   Sabine— January 11, 2012 at 2:06 am @Subhash: Interesting idea, I never thought about that. I don’t think I agree though, I think the afflux of Nobel Prices for the US after WWII is definitely due to European (in large parts German) scientists leaving Europe for the US. The later years are in my opinion a result of an increasingly better educated population.

@Guedy: As I said above, Europe suffered from severe Braindrain after WWII. This has not only an immediate influence on Nobel Prices but also a long term influence. Brilliant scientists are those who train the new generation to become brilliant scientists one day. And brains attract other brains. Why do you think Germany was able to keep the position it had for such a long time? It’s not because Germans are smarter than other people by birth (we know where that idea lead us), but there were smart people educating younger, equally smart people and attracting smart people to study there from all over Europe. It’s a tradition established over hundreds of years. The US did not have this tradition and profited from the knowledge of those fleeing Europe. It has for decades now, and we see the results on the chart above. Smart, young Americans profited from the supplementary knowledge brought to them and in turn became brilliant scientists themselves. They educated the next generation and so on… That’s the way it works.     

*   Subhash— January 11, 2012 at 9:39 am Not at all! In fact, the point I was making is that it is NOT logical to correlate just one factor with the outcome. It is far more complex than that. Books have been published by researchers on similar issues. One recent one that illuminates the complexity is titled “The Spirit Level” by Kate Pickett and Richard Wilkinson. It is about what income equality or inequality does to all kinds of indicators of human well-being. The point both of you mention that better education is the reason is absolutely on target. In fact, Guedy’s last comment confirms what I wrote some time before, that the US benefited not only from the influx of European scientists but continues to benefit from scientists from all over the world. Those “imported” scientists were not a product of US system but they found a fertile soil in our well funded and forward looking institutions of higher learning. As good as that is, it also is something to think about. At my state funded university here in the US, the Dean of Engineering once issued a directive to professors asking them to try to have at least 50% of graduate students from the United States. The professors showed him the lists of candidates applying for graduate studies. They were listed according to their merit and there were by far not enough Americans at the top to satisfy the 50% requirement. What do we think of that? I know personally that a lot of Indians are among those at the top of such lists. But I also know that they are there not BECAUSE of the good Indian system but DESPITE it. If so many of them do not go back, it is also because the institutions in India that value them are very few. The broader system there is in very bad shape. Many Indian leaders claim that the bottom heavy population pyramid of India gives India the future edge over China, where population is aging faster. But guess what? The average Chinese is better educated and better nourished than the average Indian. Will her poorly educated and undernourished young people be an asset or rather a liability? If India hopes to catch up with China there is no other way than to improve the average! A dozen or so top institutions will not do in the long run. So, ultimately it does come down to what we value: The maximum good of maximum number of people or the maximum possible achievement by only those who can.     
*   guedy— January 11, 2012 at 9:47 am I hope everybody is right.  
 I hope that with good education and less brain drain, Germany will show more Nobels, if it matters.  
 I hope that it is true that here as well, better educated post WWII Americans will educate smart people.  
 I hope that India finds its balance between encouraging some return and growing its own institutions.

I am one of those Americans who truly believe that what is best for America and the World, is for every nation, at whatever stage of development, grows its own, enlightened learning environment, and that everyone can take pride both in their national accomplishments and their contributions to the world’s progress.

I don’t need America to feel superior. I read newspapers in four languages every day precisely because I want to follow trends, and not only the negative ones.  
 I like when France takes pride in a new discovery, or Brazil becomes energy independent with sugar and aircraft manufacturing.

You’ll just have to forgive me if I react to oversimplified statements like “our system is better than yours”, which I hear from my Japanese and French friends often, or the oversimplified explanations as to why the USA does well in many areas.  
 It is what it is. I’ll enjoy my French literature, Brazilian music, German elevator, Indian Doctor, and hope to see more recognition of scientific achievements from Universities from Manila to Kiyev.

*   guedy— January 11, 2012 at 2:28 pm Subhash,  
 I do enjoy your perspective.  
 As we know, Immigration into the USA goes in waves. One only needs to observe taxi drivers in NYC to see it.  
 In the 1960s, there were many Greek cab drivers. Then they were Haitian. Then they were Israelis. Then Bengalis. Then Sikh. Then Pakistani, and now Arabs. It is not unusually to talk to a cab driver by the name of Patel or Singh and find that he has a Masters in Mathematics. One day he came to work complaining that his son was dating “an American” while there was a perfectly suitable relative in Chicago that his mother wanted him to marry.  
 Therein lies what a French writer called “les eaux melees”, the mixed waters.  
 One son married an “American” while the other married an arranged bride from Hyderabad.  
 The boys fiercely compete with us on the College Football pool, but wear 22 carat Indian gold.  
 Who wins? As a country, we do. As individuals, they do too.. Can India hope that everyone, from Brahmins to Untouchables get access to education and entrepreneurship? Of course.  
 When will it happen? This decade? This generation? Through cultivating individual achievement? Or social justice? Americans like to believe they have the best experiment in Democracy. I think India now does.  
 It is tempting for a large country to be lured into total equality, which usually means the lowest common denominator.  
 India’s best bet is to take the best of American and Chinese neo-individualism, and combine it with the power of numbers, values, education, and social responsibility.  
 Europeans by and large no longer really believe in “charity”, as in the haves giving to the have-nots.  
 They believe in a socio-economic structure that evens the playing field without the need for Charity.  
 Americans and Indians continue to believe that to whom much is given, more giving is expected.  
 some derogatorily call it “trickle-down”, but it’s not so simple. If Bill Gates gives 20 billion to causes, it is not wrong, and in retrospect, it was OK that he made 50 billion while helping put a computer in every home, which in turn may lift a rural Indian child out of ignorance and into knowledge.

Reasoning: medium
Read pages for a research assistant and follow useful links recursively. During
extraction, only the supplied page is evidence. The question defines what to look
for; parent reasoning guides navigation but is not this page's evidence.
Extraction uses the original question and current page, not the search query or
parent's hypothesis. Keep facts relevant to any part of the original question.
During navigation, a supplied local relation is a task, not evidence. Follow links
that establish or contradict it. Return when it is settled or has no useful route
here; other unresolved relations belong to the parent. Do not solve the whole
question again inside every branch.

Preserve exact relevant names and rows with their headers, values, units, dates
and scope. Never replace relevant rows with ellipses, examples or instructions to
continue the list. If all rows cannot fit, prioritize rows useful to the question
and explicitly mark omissions. A partial, restricted or truncated list is not the
complete candidate set. Missing fields are unknown. Keep relevant discoveries even
if they answer a different part of the original question.

Follow links likely to fill a candidate's missing condition or reach the required
document/year. An index is useful when it offers a concrete route to the needed
record; generic menus or keyword collections alone do not justify expansion.
Link-menu rank is only a hint: check the destination's subject and scope. If content
repeats, try a detail page or another supported route. Links outside the menu and inferred
paths on an observed site are allowed. Child notes are returned automatically;
do not copy their facts into your own note. Retain useful unvisited links even
when expansion stops.

For extraction return:

**Page:** Actual title and URL.
**Evidence:** Exact relevant facts/rows and short supporting quotes.

![Image 4: Crowd holding green‑star Esperanto flags under a sky with an airship labeled “ESPERANTO.” The words “Outside the Box” appear in bold white and green, symbolizing global thinking beyond borders.](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*0j9ckNanGWNmf-iB8RTeiw.jpeg)

The vision for world peace ignited the wish for an international language that could bring mutual understanding with little effort of learning — a dream pursued by many. Only Esperanto survived strong for 139 years and almost became the world language in 1920. Pic taken from the YouTube video _How Esperanto Almost Took Over the World_.

On July 26, 1887, a broke* young eye doctor in Warsaw published a slim booklet under the name “Doktoro Esperanto"—"the one who hopes." (*He was broke because he treated people for free. I mention it because it says something about his character.)

Zamenhof later described this inner conflict in a letter to Nikolai Borovko:

> _“I was taught that all people were brothers, and this was always a great torment to my infant mind, because around me I saw only hatred, division, and distrust.”_

It is one of the clearest windows into the psychological origin of Esperanto: a child who saw four peoples in one town, yet no bridge between them.

He called it Unua Libro, the First Book. It laid out sixteen grammar rules, a small starter dictionary, and a plan that sounded almost naive: a neutral second language, belonging to no country, that anyone could learn in months instead of years.

![Image 4: Crowd holding green‑star Esperanto flags under a sky with an airship labeled “ESPERANTO.” The words “Outside the Box” appear in bold white and green, symbolizing global thinking beyond borders.](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*0j9ckNanGWNmf-iB8RTeiw.jpeg)

The vision for world peace ignited the wish for an international language that could bring mutual understanding with little effort of learning — a dream pursued by many. Only Esperanto survived strong for 139 years and almost became the world language in 1920. Pic taken from the YouTube video _How Esperanto Almost Took Over the World_.

On July 26, 1887, a broke* young eye doctor in Warsaw published a slim booklet under the name “Doktoro Esperanto"—"the one who hopes." (*He was broke because he treated people for free. I mention it because it says something about his character.)

Zamenhof later described this inner conflict in a letter to Nikolai Borovko:

> _“I was taught that all people were brothers, and this was always a great torment to my infant mind, because around me I saw only hatred, division, and distrust.”_

It is one of the clearest windows into the psychological origin of Esperanto: a child who saw four peoples in one town, yet no bridge between them.

He called it Unua Libro, the First Book. It laid out sixteen grammar rules, a small starter dictionary, and a plan that sounded almost naive: a neutral second language, belonging to no country, that anyone could learn in months instead of years.

## The restless newyorker

# Go, get lucky!

*   [arvain](https://therestlessnewyorker.us/author/arvain/)
*   [January 16, 2026](https://therestlessnewyorker.us/2026/01/16/)
*   9:27 pm

![Image 2](https://therestlessnewyorker.us/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/daretodrive-768x1024.jpg)

The other day, I found myself in an interesting conversation when someone asked whether I was ashamed to be Hungarian. I believe they were referring to the political situation, specifically that there hasn’t been true democracy in my country for a long time — only in name. Our prime minister is well-known worldwide.

Even though the question seemed a bit offensive, I smiled because it reminded me of how complicated, painful, yet powerful this identity can be.Hungary is a small country. A troubled one, historically, and also politically, yes.

But this place is also home to a vibrant spirit of wild intellect, where unique geniuses and resilient souls work tirelessly to improve the world around them. They do boldly, and often without seeking recognition.

Long before the age of lightbulbs and smartphones, a Benedictine priest named Ányos Jedlik was experimenting with the fundamental principles of the electric motor. He also carbonated water — okay, not exactly world peace, but who doesn’t love soda?

Then came Kálmán Kandó, who helped modernize Europe’s railroads. And László Bíró, who, frustrated by leaky fountain pens, invented the ballpoint pen, still called a “biro” in many countries today.

In the 1930s, Albert Szent-Györgyi isolated vitamin C and received the Nobel Prize for it. He achieved this using paprika. Yes paprika.

John von Neumann, arguably the least Hungarian-sounding Hungarian genius, laid the groundwork for the modern computer. And in 1946, Zoltán Bay sent radar signals to the moon. Just imagine that for a second, bouncing signals off the moon, in a lab in Budapest, right after World War II.

Then there’s the Rubik’s Cube. Ernő Rubik invented it in 1974. Over 350 million cubes later, it continues to challenge minds and shape thinkers worldwide.

Even in sports, we have given the world some of its most graceful warriors, hard to choose, but I mention our swimmers, our national water polo team, and our épée fencers.

László Krasznahorkai was awarded the 2025 Nobel Prize in Literature for his compelling and visionary work that, amid apocalyptic terror, affirms the power of art. With this honor, he became the second Hungarian writer to win the Nobel in literature, after Imre Kertész in 2002. Hungarian writers and poets have achieved something remarkable: they transformed historical trauma, exile, revolution, oppression, and psychological depth into world-class literature. Many were censored, exiled, or ignored at home before being celebrated abroad—which is almost a national literary tradition.

Hungarian literature does not seek attention. It waits, deepens, and gradually shifts your perspective without you realizing, so subtly but surely. That tension—between silence and intensity—is exactly why it continues to appear on the global stage.

And now, in the 21st century, we are back in the lab again. Katalin Karikó’s groundbreaking mRNA research made the COVID-19 vaccine possible. In 2023, she finally received the Nobel Prize she had long deserved — a victory not just for science but for endurance. Genomate Health and Oncompass Medicine are pioneering digital drug assignment for Precision Oncology, offering hope to those fighting cancer in a way never seen before.

Botond Roska is restoring vision for the blind through gene therapy. And László Lovász’s lifelong dedication to elegant mathematical thought earned him the Abel Prize — the closest thing math has to a Nobel.

Hungary isn’t easy. It never has been. But it’s brilliant in that paradoxical way that rarely makes the headlines. I come from a place where people believe in ideas so much that they spend their entire lives chasing them, even when no one is watching.

And I believe that matters. I come from a place where researchers, entrepreneurs, and healthcare professionals work under nearly impossible conditions: underfunded, undervalued. Yet, somehow, they keep producing results that change lives, make the world better, and sometimes literally save it.

So, let’s face it: yes, I think maybe I am actually ashamed. Shame that our prime minister, notorious as he is, keeps managing to manipulate a nation into re-electing him every four years. I guess it’s in our blood. I let myself be manipulated, too, in my personal life, by someone who used the same tactics he does.

I truly examined my moment of hesitation before answering this question, if I am ashamed of being Hungarian.

But even with that fleeting moment of doubt, my final answer is that I’m not, actually, definitely not. I’m proud. FIERCELY proud.

Even if, in my mother’s words, I’ve “failed as a Hungarian” because I moved abroad and see my future in America. For me, so far, this is the place where if you work hard and hold on long enough, someone will notice. Someone will care. And that, too, matters. Honestly, this matters the most to me.

Here’s a less-discussed aspect of people proudly mentioning our Hungarian geniuses: many of these brilliant minds didn’t achieve great success because of Hungary- unfortunately, they succeed to thrived in spite of it.

Too often, they had to leave.  
To secure funding, to earn credibility, to have the freedom to think, to simply survive.

Karikó, Neumann, Bíró, Gábor Dénes, Szent-Györgyi — just to name a few — all received recognition abroad, mostly in the U.S., where openness, curiosity, and room to grow existed. fail, and room to begin again, and again, and again, until the world-changing results were born.

So…Lucky?

Was I born with six degrees of knowledge, or because four languages were somehow pre-installed into my brain? Because fourteen books just wrote themselves, or because someone handed me a PhD like a party favor?

Are you f@cking kidding me? Wake up.

This wasn’t luck.

This was decades of relentless work. It was blood, sweat, and salt — sometimes all at once. It meant working day and night, literally, through migraines and heartbreaks. It involved missing birthdays, canceling dinners, and writing “sorry, I can’t make it” for the hundredth time. It led to losing friends. It meant walking outside in joggers, hoping no one would see me, because I collapsed into bed at 4:40AM exactly as I was, fully dressed, and at 6 AM, I woke up like that and went out to walk the dog. I looked like sh@t and hadn’t showered all day.

This was running on caffeine and prayer. This was dry eyes and blurry vision at 3 AM, with pages lit only by screen glow. This was saying goodbye to moments with people I love because I had deadlines to meet, lives to study, papers to peer-review, patients to care for, and futures to build into existence. This was collapsing on the floor, crying because I couldn’t do it anymore, and then doing it anyway.

This was burning out, breaking down, and getting back up, again and again and again, as always, “just one more time”.

Last year, I’ve been doing all of this while navigating fear, trauma, and violations of my safety, unable to sleep, troubled by nightmares and flashbacks, exhausted like never before, while still showing up to work, writing, leading, and caring.

So no. I don’t go by luck. I’m not lucky, just determined as hell.

You call it luck, I call it work, I call it dedication. And if you put in the work too, you just might “get lucky” yourself.

Go get lucky, girl.

## THE AMERICAN SOCIOLOGIST: EDITORIAL STATEMENT 

The decision of the Executive Committee and Council of the American Sociological Association to publish The American Sociologist is a landmark in the development, not only of the Association, but of sociology as a dis-cipline, if this he understood to include not only the scientific character of sociology, but also the social organization of its activities. The company of those entitled to call themselves sociologists in a professional sense has grown very rapidly in the last generation—there are now 3,300 active members and fellows of this Association, among nearly 9,000 members of all categories, and the number of our colleagues in other countries is also rapidly increasing. 

For some twenty-six years the Review has served as the primary official organ of the Association for the publication of the scholarly output of its members and has also served as the channel for the publication of official reports and proceedings, news and notes, obituaries and other such materials. In 1958 under the Editorship of Charles Page, the Review introduced a Section on the Profession, which went beyond these official materials and more utilitarian news items, to introduce serious discussion of problems of the profession, its functions, its internal affairs, and its relation to the non-sociological community. 

However, the pressures on the Review have been growing, and the moment seemed to have arrived when it was both desirable and feasible to differentiate the two main functions, that of the publication of scientific and scholarly output and that of serving as an organ of information and discussion for the professional concerns of sociologists as a social collectivity. We expect that there will be an important area of overlap, namely where these affairs become themselves the object of research attention. Construed broadly this would include a considerable range of work on higher education, the special develop-ments of the social sciences, their relations to each other and to other dis-ciplines, the teaching of sociology to communicate to their colleagues. It is hoped that more space for such communications will be available than there has been in the Review. The Editor and his colleagues on the Editorial Board cordially invite members of the Association, and others, as well, to submit communications for this purpose. It seems particularly important that we have a healthy and representative flow of such communications, because the profession, in general, and the Association, in particular, are involved in important processes of growth and change at the present time and will he for

With respect to this centrally important function the Editor will inevitably be faced with difficulties. The avail-able space will probably not be sufficient to publish all communications received or to publish them in full. Hence a process of selection will become necessary. Furthermore, it is to be expected that questions of suitability, as well as volume, will arise. In order to ensure the greatest pos-sible fairness in both these respects, the Editor will call on the members of his Editorial Board to review cases in a manner parallel to that in which Associate Editors have served in the other three Journals of the Association. 

The main feature of this first issue of the Sociologist 

is the long-awaited Report of the Committee on Organiza-tional Relationships, of which Robert E. L. Fans has been Chairman, with its Preface by the President of the As-sociation, Wilbert E. Moore. The recommendations made in this Report raise many far-reaching issues on which members of the Association will wish to express their opinions. The Editor, therefore, not only particularly invites communications bearing on these recommenda-tions, but will give them high priority for the two issues (February and May, 1966) which will appear before the Report is formally submitted to the Council for action. Communications may of course be submitted directly to the officers and other members of the Council, but those published in the Sociologist will have a much wider audience. 

The second primary responsibility of sociologists as a group derives from the fact that they are professional students of societies, including the one to which they belong. Furthermore, more than any of our sister-dis-ciplines, sociology occupies a central role in understand-ing the place of the social sciences generally and of sociology, in particular, in the society of which we are a part. We are, therefore, committed to an especially im-portant and difficult problem of self-study and under-standing, since, in a sense in which this is not true for natural scientists, it is our professional job to include the study of ourselves in our own program of work. 

Research output of this nature will, as noted, constitute the core of the limited function which The American 

Sociologist will discharge in the publication of scholarly work. It would not, however, be advisable to define this sphere too rigidly in advance. We feel that The American 

Sociologist should deal not only with the sociological profession as such but with its "organizational environ-ment" in a variety of ways. The appropriate limits will have to be defined in the course of experience. 

There will, in this context, be a problem of overlap, 

both with the Review and with Sociology of Education, 

and, to some degree, with Sociometry. The Editor wishes to make clear that neither he nor the Association wishes to impose obligation on any author to publish such material in this Journal rather than one of the others. An author should submit his article to whichever Journal 

seems most appropriate to him and it will then be a matter for editorial decision in the usual manner how the article is dealt with. Your Editor, however, expects to keep in close touch with the Editors of the other Journals in this respect. Furthermore, he hopes that a sufficient number of high quality articles will be submitted, so that the limited space available for them can be fruitfully used. 

The Editorial Board has conic to the conclusion that it would not be advisable for The American Sociologist 

to attempt to conduct a regular book review section. It will not review books routinely, and for that reason no book review editor has been appointed. We do, however, fully recognize that there is an output of literature of which the Sociologist ought to take cognizance, and that this is likely to grow. For the present, however, we expect to keep on the alert for especially significant publica-tions, and to give them such attention as seems appro-priate, from brief notices to a review article. It seems likely that there will he clusters of two, three or four significant publications hearing on our interests, which will merit the latter level of attention. Had, for example, this Journal been in publication at the time of the ap-

pearance of Sibley's Education of Sociologists in the United States, a comprehensive review article would have been mandatory. The Editor will appreciate any sugges-tions from our readers about the literature which ought to be discussed in our columns. 

One further point. Since The American Sociologist is a rather different kind of Journal from the other three published by the Association, devoted to the interests and concerns of a professional group, it seems appropriate that its Editor should plan to use his office to take occasion from time to time to formulate questions which seem appropriate to its functions, and to comment on a variety of pertinent issues. For this purpose it is pro-posed that there will ordinarily be an "Editor's Column" in each issue, which will be used for this purpose. Hence, the present statement is not a single effort after which the Editor's concerns will work wholly behind the scenes, but is the first of a series expected to continue as long as he is Editor. In interpreting this column, however, it should be kept clearly in mind by the Reader that the Editor in no way speaks for the American Sociological Association; he is neither an officer nor, on any other basis, a member of the Council. His is only one opinion which, however, by virtue of the Council having entrusted him with the present responsibility, he is privileged to express. 

Since the publication of The American Sociologist is such an entirely new venture, both for the Association and for your Editor and his colleagues on the Editorial Board, we will have to feel our way and will certainly introduce changes from time to time. For this reason again we will particularly welcome criticisms and sug-gestions from our readers. Though it would be incom-patible with our responsibilities to promise their adoption in advance, we do promise that all of them will be given full and respectful consideration. 

November, 1965 REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON ORGANIZATIONAL RELATIONSHIPS 

## Prefatory Note: by the President of the Anierican Sociological Association 

The report presented here is that of the Committee on Organizational Relationships, appointed by President Everett C. Hughes in 1963. Widely referred to as the "Fans Committee Report," particularly during the 1965 Annual Meeting in Chicago, when, unfortunately, it became a kind of "little black box," the report is in fact the truly joint product of an extremely able, conscien-tious, and hard-working group of our colleagues across the country. President Hughes chose this committee with great care, and I know from my limited contacts with it as a collectivity and my many contacts with its members that it was not so constituted as to he a kind of mindless Greek chorus for its chairman, Professor Fans. 

The views of members of the Association on all sorts of matters differ widely and most of these differences were ardently advocated within the Committee. Many of its recommendations come down strongly on one side of an organizational question. Others represent compromises among reasonable differences among reasonable men. 

Let me first thank the Committee for its labors in our common interests. I thank them as a member of this As-sociation, who happens to he in a position to get these few words into print, even more than as its current Presi-dent. I know of no Committee in recent history that har taken on such an important mission or performed it so well. 

I had the privilege of testifying before the Committee at its next-to-last meeting, and came with prepared testimony. I first commented to my colleagues that they would appreciate the temporal irony of my message, as President-Elect. The main burden of my comment was that the office of the presidency should he downgraded in several particulars. There is no reason to suppose that incoming presidents will he familiar with the Associa-tion's practices, with the common law of precedent. The written statutes must necessarily be a poor guide to operations, and I hope that tidy, bureaucratic minds will mostly leave matters that way. But various presidential powers appeared to me improper. .A few examples must suffice: The President, under current legislation, names the Committee on Nominations and Elections, with fifteen members, the sole binding restriction being that no less than four nor more than five members should continue from the preceding year. (Incidentally, I believe that I was illegally nominated.) There are some addi-tional, sanctionless pieties about the committee being "broadly representative of the membership of the As-sociation, taking into account the fields of specialization and the geographical distribution of the members." No 

President has yet been impeached for non-compliance with these prescriptions andindeed we have no mech-anism for removing miscreants—hut I suggest that the solution is to remove the responsibility from the Presi-dent. I believe that this is a case where a peculiar dynasty could be perpetuated; cure for that defect is one of the virtues of the Committee's proposals. 

I have also observed that currently only two members of a five-member Program Committee are named by the Council, but here precedent is also wrong. In effect, the President-Elect has named the two members, ratified by the Council. But surely we should reconsider that situa-tion. If I may speak firmly as the current President, it is not the President's program but the Association's pro-gram, and we should see to it that the President's hand is steadied by suitable representation of the Association's multifarious interests, to protect ourselves from able, strong-willed, but quite parochial presidents (a highly probable combination of character traits). 

Let me now speak bluntly of certain political issues, though these are the matters that I should hope would be debated at considerable length in open conclave. (1) The proposals of the Fans Committee seek to reaffirm and restore membership participation and responsibility in the selection not only of governing mechanisms, but also of the process of nomination. I have heard some talk to the effect that this report is a method of consolidating the control of a clique or cabal or establishment. Read the proposals, please, with care, and then ask what bear-ing they have on such a suggestion. (2) No one wants to weaken regional societies, which have important func-tions to perform. I am an active member of my regional society. but I do not think of it as either a wholly-owned subsidiary of the ASA, or, on the other hand, as con-stituting a "regional bloc" in ASA decisions. Most of our reasonable differences within the ASA have little to do with geography: preferences in style of sociological work, views on the selection and accountability of technical officers of the Association, scientism versus activism as the proper stance of the sociologist. These issues cut deep, and will remain, but I doubt that they have any sub-stantial relevance to the operation of regional groups. I hope that regional societies will not get organizationally more closely integrated with the ASA, other than through the advisory committee proposed here. Let pluralism pre-vail. (3) 1 believe we should continue and perhaps ex-pand the recognition of affiliated societies, primarily as a basis of program cooperation. This year in Chicago not only did the Society for the Stud )' of Social Problems 

> The American Sociologist

meet just prior to the Association's convention, as usual, but so did the Rural Sociological Society and the Anier-jean Catholic Sociological Society. So, in effect, did the newly formed Law and Society Association. The Sociolog-ical Research Association always meets at the time of the Association's convention but does not appear on the prograni. As long as the actual governing of the Associa-tion is not at issue, program cooperation with separately organized groups would seem mutually beneficial. 

I promised to be blunt, and I have fulfilled that promise. But let me he more positive: let us have all sorts of associations that represent identifiable common in-terests.'and let those associations have their own ways of finding what unites them. But let us have an American Sociological Association, with a membership that is entirely individual, dedicated only to our common con-cerns as sociologists, and not filtered through regional identification, ideological stands, or substantive spe-cialties. 

Now, let me say a word about procedure. I propose the following: During this year Dr. Edmund Volkart, the Association's Executive Officer, and I hope to meet with every regional society in an open membership meeting. We hope to be joined in those sessions by the one or more members of the regional association who served on the Committee on Organizational Relationships, members who can therefore therefore testify concerning the "legislative history" of particular proposals. Subsequent to these regional meetings, but before the 1966 Annual Meeting, I hope it will he possible for the current Council of the American Sociological Association to meet in extra-ordinary session, undisturbed b y other business, for full discussion of the proposals, point by point. 

In addition to the invitation extended by the Editor 

of The American Sociologist to submit comients for possible publication in this journal, I should welcome expression of view's from an )' member of the Association to inc personally. You may address me at Russell Sage Foundation, 230 Park Avenue, New York, N.Y. 10017. I cannot promise an extended bilateral correspondence, as time and energy have their limits. But I can promise referral to lii)' superiors, the membership of the Council of this Association. 

All changes in the Constitution and By-laws, recoin-mended b y the Council, will, in accord with the provi-sions of the Constitution. be submitted to vote by the entire voting membership of the Association.

> REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE

The American Sociological Associa-tion is sixty years old, but it has been a large organization for only a rela-tively short time. As late as 1939 the total membership was less than one thousand, and its routine business was handled by an unpaid member serving in his spare time as Secretary and Treasurer. The budget was small and simple. Total expenses for the fiscal year ending December 14. 1939 were reported to be $7,893 1 of which $6,277 was allocated to The American Socio-logical Review, and only $1,615 for all other expenses of the organization. 

The conduct of the scholarly and organizational affairs of the Society in 

1939 was also relatively simple. De-cisions were made by a small Executive Committee and by the three Business Meetings that were scheduled at each annual convention. Election of officers took place at the third Business Meet-ing, from nominations presented only the day before, and the total number of 

ballots cast would usually he in the neighborhood of 150. 

Rapid growth of ASA membership occurred after the Second World War and has continued to the present time, with no prospect of early leveling. It was not until 1946 that the Society established criteria for voting member-ship; in the previous 41 years any per-son willing to pay the modest dues could be a full member of the Amer-ican Sociological Society and have a voice and vote in its actions and poli-cies. At the Business Meeting of De-cember 29, 1946, a proposal for classi-fication of members as Active, Joint, Life, and Emeritus, and Associate. Stu-dent, and Honorary, the latter three not having voting rights, was presented. The recommendation was adopted in the Business Meeting of the following day. The size of the vote is not recorded in the published minutes. but the vote on a controversial resolution at the 

same session shows less than 100 bal-lots cast. 

In 1949 the Executive Committee, in view of the growth of membership to 

2,450 in 1948, and the increasing com-plexity of the business, as indicated by an annual budget of over $20,000. 

established a Committee on Reorganiza-tion. The work of this committee led to a request to the Carnegie Corporation for a grant to support reorganizational activities of the Society. The grant was made, andan enlarged committee was appointed. It was this reorganization process that first established a head-quarters with an Executive Officer with a paid staff, although for some years the budget for this function re'nlained in a meagre 12-15 thousand dollar range. A new Constitution was adopted in 1951 by a mail vote of the member-ship. It is this Constitution, with sub-sequent amendments, under which the Association is now operating. 

Important adaptive changes were in-

November, 1965 5troduced by the 1951 reorganization. The governing responsibility was placed in a Council and an Executive Commit-tee consisting of members of the Coun-cil. Power to act in the name of the Association was specifically removed from the Business Meetings. The new Council consisted of the principal officers, who were ex officio members; six members elected at large by the membership in a mail ballot, and repre-sentatives from each of the regional and affiliated societies, elected by those societies. Divisions and Sections, with responsibilities for some of the annual program at the convention, were omitted. Anion., the amendments of importance, in following years, were the establishment of tile category of Fel-lows, and the re-introduction of Sections on a more systematic basis than that of earlier Sections. 

The total membership in 1951 was under 4,000, and the annual budget ap-proximately $44000. The membership is now over 8,000, and the budget about to cross the million dollar mark. In place of a part-time Executive Officer with a secretary or two, the Association now has a large and expanding suite of offices and employees, with a full-time Executive Officer. The business of the Association has multiplied, with four journals instead of one (and prob-ably others to be established soon), a monograph series, several large research grants, and an expanding set of impor-tant professional activities. 

Current Problems of the Organization 

The present Council has thirty-two members. Recent experience has con-vinced many of its members, and all of the Committee on Organizational Rela-tionships, that the body is too large to handle adequately the amount and complexity of business. It has difficulty in covering tile items on its agenda at the time of the annual meeting, and it is too large and therefore expensive to convene at other times of the year. Much of its work is almost perfunc-torily delegated to other committees, often with power to act. The size of the Council makes it almost impossible to examine any question thoroughly while in session. 

The membership of the Council, as established by the 1951 Constitution, produces a condition of unequal repre-sentation of the membership. The affili-ated societies represented oil Coun-cil are greatly unequal in size, and have varying proportions of their own men-hers who arc not members of the Amer-

ican Sociological Association, but who, nevertheless, take part in selecting its governing body. Members of the Asso-ciation may belong to none, one, two, or three or more affiliated societies, and thereby increase their voting influence. Some sociological organizations, such as the Sociological Research Associa-tion, the Canadian Sociological Asso-ciation, and the Catholic Sociological Society, are not represented at all. 

A further imbalance exists by virtue of the fact that while two members of the Council represent substantive, rather than regional, interests--those of the Rural Sociological Society and the Society for the Study of Social Prob-lems—there is no representation on tile Council of such other large subject mat-ter interests as are represented in the Sections. In order to eliminate this in-equity in the influence of substantive organizations, negotiations were under-taken in recent years to induce the two affiliated societies named above to be-conic Sections, but both organizations declined, understandably since each has a well-established function, mem-bership, and journal. 

Concern with these unsatisfactory conditions has been felt for more than ten years and discussion in subcommit-tees of the Council, in the Executive Committee, and no doubt extensively in informal circles, has been continuous. During his recent term as president, Everett C. Hughes published in the August 1962 issue of the Review, a co-gent discussion of the issue of the rela-tion of the Association to its members. He pointed out that there are federated organizations, like the American Coun-cil of Learned Societies, which were founded by member societies. Others, and the American Sociological Associa-tion has always been of this type, were established by and composed of individ-uals. President Hughes invited discus-sion of the course the Association should take in relation to its affiliated societies, stating his preference, 110w-

ever, that ". . . we adhere to the notion of a society of individual sociologists"— a view shared by the members of this committee. 

Presentation of the above issue has revealed that many members of the Association and of affiliated societies do not know the history of their origins. All of these organizations in fact had completely independent origins. The The American Sociological Association, founded in 1905, is by far the oldest. The first of the affiliated societies was established about a quarter of a cen-tury later. Each of the latter was organ-ized by individuals interested in their 

stated purposes, and none was in any way organized by the Association. The only formal link ever established be-tween them was the 1951 unilateral provision of the Association allowing each affiliated affiliated society to elect one mem-ber of the Association Council. No tax, contribution, or other service was asked or received in return for this, and no control by ASA over any aspect of an affiliated society was attempted. Never-theless, some members of affiliated so-cieties have come to conceive of their representation on the Council as a mat-ter of right, grounded in time-honored tradition rather than a recent constitu-tional innovation, and some representa-tives on the Council have shown indica-tions of conceiving of their duty as representing the special interests of the society that elected them, rather than representing the interests of the As-sociation and its entire membership. 

Some members have also expressed apprehension that the large and un-wieldy Council produces conditions which favor the domination of Associa-tion action, the annual program, and the Committee appointments, by a self-perpetuating power clique, against which tile representation of affiliated so-cieties on the Council was held to be a desirable protection. 

The present committee has devoted much time to study of the arguments andevidence relating to these beliefs, and is of the opinion that no conclu-sions can he drawn that would be con-vincing to all members of the Associa-tion. Quite independently, however, of the validity of these beliefs, it is desira-ble to assure wide and equitable par-ticipation in the affairs of the Associa-tion, and this objective is reflected throughout the present recommenda-tions, especiall y those connected with the Committee on Nominations and the Committee oil 

President Hughes, early in his term, announced his intention of appointing a committee to make a general study and produce recommendations on the form of organization of the Association. He established the present committee in the spring of 1963, with one member, Stanley tidy, added in the fall of 1964. The original assignment for tile commit-tee was broad. Additional requests from the Council further widened its scope, eventually to include in effect any aspect of the constitutional form of tile Association. 

The committee members present at the 1963 convention in Los Angeles held a brief meeting to discuss ways of operating. At the same convention, two general open sessions for all ASA mem-

Tile American Sociologist hers were held, to invite comments, sug-gestions, criticisms, and questions. Further mail contributions from mem-bers were invited. 

The committee then worked by cor-respondence through the fall and win-ter, and held a one-day meeting at the Association headquarters in March, 1964. Further correspondence con-tinued during the following year, and an additional meeting was held at the Montreal convention. At the same time discussions were held between the com-mittee chairman and the ASA Council, as well as with members attending the convention. In the late winter of 1964 it was the consensus of the members that it would be possible to complete the major decisions in one more face-to-face meeting, and so a final two-day session took place on May 21-22, 1965 in Washington, D.C. This report pre-sents the judgments resulting from the entire two-year process. 

During the period of its labors. the committee has had the benefit of con-sultation with several past and future presidents and other officers, with officers and members of affiliated so-cieties, and with individual ASA mem-hers. It has also had the benefit of valu-able information and assistance from the Executive Officer, Gresham Sykes, and the staff of the Washington office. Many criticisms and suggestions were made and examined at length. Some ingenious ideas were found to be im-practical for such a body as the ASA, and some criticisms of present opera-tions were discovered to be unjustified. III however, the committee benefited greatly from the wide range of communications received. Many sug-gestions which were not adopted by the committee were thoroughly considered in detail, including the idea of Council representation by regions rather than by regional associations, the concept of a two-house parliament, the sug-gestion that political parties he formed, and various others. Further sugges-tions, such as the maintenance of the one-member-one-vote principle in the electoral process, are among the recom-mendations of the committee. Still other suggestions, such as the dee-tion of the Association nominating com-mittee by the affiliated societies, were not adopted, but materially influenced the committee's recommendations. 

After careful consideration of these various suggestions and criticisms, the committee has arrived at the recom-mendations summarized below and stated in a proposed Constitution. It is the unanimous judgment of the commit-

tee that the purposes of the Association and the flourishing of sociology would be advanced by the adoption of the pro-posed changes, and that these changes would serve to maintain an appropriate balance among the varied interests of the members. The proposals meet both major criticisms of the present struc-ture by arranging a balance between efficiency (through a small Council for policy making) and responsibility to the varied interests of the membership.

The formal preparation of Social Scientists in fields other than their own provides a basis for analyzing inter-relations among disciplines. Cross-disci-plinary fields of study generally suggest the development of scholars equipped to bridge the lacunae between fields. Obviously, this is only one of several ways of examining interrelations among Social Sciences. Several recent studies have produced relevant data. 

There is an historical and logical basis for dividing intellectual disci-plines into the Natural Sciences, the Social Sciences, and the Humanities.1 The remaining Arts and Professions generally are concerned more with applying knowledge than with its crea-tion. These areas and their many sub-divisions provide the basis for com-partmentalizing knowledge, itself, for organizing the educational establish-ment, for identifying occupational spe-cialties, and for other aspects of pro-fessionalization.

While there are notable failures and some successes to record for these ap-proaches, each field continues to make unique contributions to knowledge of human behavior and socio-cultural sys-tems, and borrowing of method, theory, and results one from the other has never been greater than now. As time passes we are seeing more evidence that the Social Sciences are converging toward common understandings.4 

Interrelations among the Social Sci-ences may be analyzed in three con-texts: 1) substantively, through study of the extent that the disciplines con-tribute concepts, hypotheses, evidence, etc., to the explanation of behavior; 2) organizationally, through studying the interrelations among curricula, courses of study, degree requirements, and among institutional subdivisions; and 3) individually, by analyzing the extent that individuals have bridged gaps between fields through their varied experiences, particularly educational experiences. 

This paper examines one kind of evidence on the individual basis of integration among the Social Sciences: formal educational experiences repre-sented by degrees in major subjects, and by minors and majors of bac-calaureates. 

The thesis: functional integration among the Social Sciences is taking place through cross-disciplinary aca-demic experiences of students as they pass through successive degree levels in the educational system. This is char-acterized by the cross-disciplinary fields of study of students at three levels of educational attainment. While only generally indicative of the integration that is developing, the data nevertheless provide one tangible basis for examin-ing interrelations among Social Science disciplines. For example, the experience of a person with a baccalaureate major in one Social Science discipline and a master's degree major in another repre-sents a functional relationship between two fields. Considering the cross-disciplinary academic experience discussed above, doctorate recipients in Sociology, Anthropology, and Political Science are broadly based in other Social Sciences. > SUMMARY

The cross-disciplinar y formal aca-demic experiences of students who have achieved degrees at the three degree levels have provided a picture of the interrelations among Social Sciences and between the Social Sciences and other disciplinary areas. By these gross measures. the Social Sciences are largely independent of the Natural Sciences and Mathematics, but have closer ties to the Arts and Professions and Humanities. Much needs to be (lone if the disciplines, skills, and rigor of the Natural Sciences and Mathematics are to be grafted to the Social Sciences, as Sibley and others have suggested, through means of formal educational experiences. 

Among themselves, the Social Sci-ences are tied together in many ways which these data reflect but weakly. While Psychology, History and Eco-nomics predominate numerically, Soci-ology, Anthropology, and Political Sci-ence have strong linkage to other Social Sciences. Ample opportunity exists for each field to encourage formal cross-disciplinary educational experiences, with the objective of bene-fiting from the unique contributions of each in understanding various sectors of human behavior. The encouragement of such sequences in individuals tends toward a convergence in knowledge among Social Sciences. > EDITORIAL NOTE

For this particular issue, the first place in the section on Communications to the Editor, is given to two recent cases of cancellation of contracts for the support of sociological research on the part of agencies of the Federal Government, in both cases, as it hap-pens, branches of the Department of Defense. The first is the "Project CAMELOT" which was initiated and supported, through the American Uni-versity in Washington, by the Special Operations Research Office (SORO). This case has been given rather wide publicity, including, besides the daily press, the statement in Science (10 September, 1965, PP . 1211-1213, signed by John Walsh). The research involved concerned the sources of potential in-stability in social systems, including the relations to political regimes, and was concentrated on Latin American Societies. 

The second case was that of a con-tract by the Air Force with the Russell Sage Foundation, for a study of a sample of officers in the Air Force in respects in which they compared with samples of several civilian occupations, in a combination of personality and social attitudes and traits. 

Both projects touched sensitive areas, on the one hand, the internal political tensions of foreign countries; on the other hand, the private personal con-cerns of the individual subjects. The problems of just what lines are to be drawn between professionally objective research orientation, and some kind of possibly illegitimate intervention of the social researcher, on the one hand, into the political concerns of the society in question; on the other, the "personal" concerns of the subjects, involves deli-cate questions of professional ethics for the social science investigator, and of the responsibilities of granting or coin-missioning agencies, be they govern-mental or private, for considering the standards of the professional groups whose cooperation is requested, and the security of the professional positions in which investigators are placed. 

We hereby present brief communi-cations on these two subjects, first by Jessie Bernard, who has been directly involved in "Project CAMELOT," and by Theodore D. Kemper, about the 

Russell Sage—Air Force Contract. Both are conceived as initial state-ments, designed, in the first instance, to inform readers of The American 

Sociologist of the most salient facts of the case, and, in the second, to state briefly a few of the salient issues of the relations of professional sociologists to the government agencies in question. These statements are—in both cases by the suggestion of the Editor—meant, not to state full and definitive cases for a position on the issues, but rather to initiate discussion, by summarizing facts and formulating issues. It is ex-pected that considerable discussion will follow on these initial statements in both cases. The Editor invites corre-spondents to follow up these initial statements by contributing relevant elaborations, comments and sugges-tions. 

As a word of caution it may finally be noted that, with each such large 

topic opened up, The American Sociol-

ogist is likely to face a future difficulty of finding space for the communications which may be expected to come. The readership is merely warned that these two eases of government contract re-lations with sociological researchers, illustrate only one of a large variety of fields in which issues of comparable importance to our membership can be expected to arise. The place these cases are given in our initial issue is not a harbinger of the permanent position of this particular kind of issue, but rather an attempt to give issues salient at the moment of publication their due, while keeping open an opportunity for other issues to compete for attention as they arise in time coining months and years.

The decision of the Executive Committee and Council of the American Sociological Association to publish The American Sociologist is a landmark in the development, not only of the Association, but of sociology as a dis-cipline, if this he understood to include not only the scientific character of sociology, but also the social organization of its activities. The company of those entitled to call themselves sociologists in a professional sense has grown very rapidly in the last generation—there are now 3,300 active members and fellows of this Association, among nearly 9,000 members of all categories, and the number of our colleagues in other countries is also rapidly increasing. 

For some twenty-six years the Review has served as the primary official organ of the Association for the publication of the scholarly output of its members and has also served as the channel for the publication of official reports and proceedings, news and notes, obituaries and other such materials. In 1958 under the Editorship of Charles Page, the Review introduced a Section on the Profession, which went beyond these official materials and more utilitarian news items, to introduce serious discussion of problems of the profession, its functions, its internal affairs, and its relation to the non-sociological community. 

However, the pressures on the Review have been growing, and the moment seemed to have arrived when it was both desirable and feasible to differentiate the two main functions, that of the publication of scientific and scholarly output and that of serving as an organ of information and discussion for the professional concerns of sociologists as a social collectivity. We expect that there will be an important area of overlap, namely where these affairs become themselves the object of research attention. Construed broadly this would include a considerable range of work on higher education, the special develop-ments of the social sciences, their relations to each other and to other dis-ciplines, the teaching of sociology to communicate to their colleagues. It is hoped that more space for such communications will be available than there has been in the Review. The Editor and his colleagues on the Editorial Board cordially invite members of the Association, and others, as well, to submit communications for this purpose. It seems particularly important that we have a healthy and representative flow of such communications, because the profession, in general, and the Association, in particular, are involved in important processes of growth and change at the present time and will he for

With respect to this centrally important function the Editor will inevitably be faced with difficulties. The avail-able space will probably not be sufficient to publish all communications received or to publish them in full. Hence a process of selection will become necessary. Furthermore, it is to be expected that questions of suitability, as well as volume, will arise. In order to ensure the greatest pos-sible fairness in both these respects, the Editor will call on the members of his Editorial Board to review cases in a manner parallel to that in which Associate Editors have served in the other three Journals of the Association. 

The main feature of this first issue of the Sociologist 

is the long-awaited Report of the Committee on Organiza-tional Relationships, of which Robert E. L. Fans has been Chairman, with its Preface by the President of the As-sociation, Wilbert E. Moore. The recommendations made in this Report raise many far-reaching issues on which members of the Association will wish to express their opinions. The Editor, therefore, not only particularly invites communications bearing on these recommenda-tions, but will give them high priority for the two issues (February and May, 1966) which will appear before the Report is formally submitted to the Council for action. Communications may of course be submitted directly to the officers and other members of the Council, but those published in the Sociologist will have a much wider audience. 

The second primary responsibility of sociologists as a group derives from the fact that they are professional students of societies, including the one to which they belong. Furthermore, more than any of our sister-dis-ciplines, sociology occupies a central role in understand-ing the place of the social sciences generally and of sociology, in particular, in the society of which we are a part. We are, therefore, committed to an especially im-portant and difficult problem of self-study and under-standing, since, in a sense in which this is not true for natural scientists, it is our professional job to include the study of ourselves in our own program of work. 

Research output of this nature will, as noted, constitute the core of the limited function which The American 

Sociologist will discharge in the publication of scholarly work. It would not, however, be advisable to define this sphere too rigidly in advance. We feel that The American 

Sociologist should deal not only with the sociological profession as such but with its "organizational environ-ment" in a variety of ways. The appropriate limits will have to be defined in the course of experience. 

There will, in this context, be a problem of overlap, 

both with the Review and with Sociology of Education, 

and, to some degree, with Sociometry. The Editor wishes to make clear that neither he nor the Association wishes to impose obligation on any author to publish such material in this Journal rather than one of the others. An author should submit his article to whichever Journal 

seems most appropriate to him and it will then be a matter for editorial decision in the usual manner how the article is dealt with. Your Editor, however, expects to keep in close touch with the Editors of the other Journals in this respect. Furthermore, he hopes that a sufficient number of high quality articles will be submitted, so that the limited space available for them can be fruitfully used. 

The Editorial Board has conic to the conclusion that it would not be advisable for The American Sociologist 

to attempt to conduct a regular book review section. It will not review books routinely, and for that reason no book review editor has been appointed. We do, however, fully recognize that there is an output of literature of which the Sociologist ought to take cognizance, and that this is likely to grow. For the present, however, we expect to keep on the alert for especially significant publica-tions, and to give them such attention as seems appro-priate, from brief notices to a review article. It seems likely that there will he clusters of two, three or four significant publications hearing on our interests, which will merit the latter level of attention. Had, for example, this Journal been in publication at the time of the ap-

pearance of Sibley's Education of Sociologists in the United States, a comprehensive review article would have been mandatory. The Editor will appreciate any sugges-tions from our readers about the literature which ought to be discussed in our columns. 

One further point. Since The American Sociologist is a rather different kind of Journal from the other three published by the Association, devoted to the interests and concerns of a professional group, it seems appropriate that its Editor should plan to use his office to take occasion from time to time to formulate questions which seem appropriate to its functions, and to comment on a variety of pertinent issues. For this purpose it is pro-posed that there will ordinarily be an "Editor's Column" in each issue, which will be used for this purpose. Hence, the present statement is not a single effort after which the Editor's concerns will work wholly behind the scenes, but is the first of a series expected to continue as long as he is Editor. In interpreting this column, however, it should be kept clearly in mind by the Reader that the Editor in no way speaks for the American Sociological Association; he is neither an officer nor, on any other basis, a member of the Council. His is only one opinion which, however, by virtue of the Council having entrusted him with the present responsibility, he is privileged to express. 

Since the publication of The American Sociologist is such an entirely new venture, both for the Association and for your Editor and his colleagues on the Editorial Board, we will have to feel our way and will certainly introduce changes from time to time. For this reason again we will particularly welcome criticisms and sug-gestions from our readers. Though it would be incom-patible with our responsibilities to promise their adoption in advance, we do promise that all of them will be given full and respectful consideration. 

November, 1965 REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON ORGANIZATIONAL RELATIONSHIPS 

## Prefatory Note: by the President of the Anierican Sociological Association 

The report presented here is that of the Committee on Organizational Relationships, appointed by President Everett C. Hughes in 1963. Widely referred to as the "Fans Committee Report," particularly during the 1965 Annual Meeting in Chicago, when, unfortunately, it became a kind of "little black box," the report is in fact the truly joint product of an extremely able, conscien-tious, and hard-working group of our colleagues across the country. President Hughes chose this committee with great care, and I know from my limited contacts with it as a collectivity and my many contacts with its members that it was not so constituted as to he a kind of mindless Greek chorus for its chairman, Professor Fans. 

The views of members of the Association on all sorts of matters differ widely and most of these differences were ardently advocated within the Committee. Many of its recommendations come down strongly on one side of an organizational question. Others represent compromises among reasonable differences among reasonable men. 

Let me first thank the Committee for its labors in our common interests. I thank them as a member of this As-sociation, who happens to he in a position to get these few words into print, even more than as its current Presi-dent. I know of no Committee in recent history that har taken on such an important mission or performed it so well. 

I had the privilege of testifying before the Committee at its next-to-last meeting, and came with prepared testimony. I first commented to my colleagues that they would appreciate the temporal irony of my message, as President-Elect. The main burden of my comment was that the office of the presidency should he downgraded in several particulars. There is no reason to suppose that incoming presidents will he familiar with the Associa-tion's practices, with the common law of precedent. The written statutes must necessarily be a poor guide to operations, and I hope that tidy, bureaucratic minds will mostly leave matters that way. But various presidential powers appeared to me improper. .A few examples must suffice: The President, under current legislation, names the Committee on Nominations and Elections, with fifteen members, the sole binding restriction being that no less than four nor more than five members should continue from the preceding year. (Incidentally, I believe that I was illegally nominated.) There are some addi-tional, sanctionless pieties about the committee being "broadly representative of the membership of the As-sociation, taking into account the fields of specialization and the geographical distribution of the members." No 

President has yet been impeached for non-compliance with these prescriptions andindeed we have no mech-anism for removing miscreants—hut I suggest that the solution is to remove the responsibility from the Presi-dent. I believe that this is a case where a peculiar dynasty could be perpetuated; cure for that defect is one of the virtues of the Committee's proposals. 

I have also observed that currently only two members of a five-member Program Committee are named by the Council, but here precedent is also wrong. In effect, the President-Elect has named the two members, ratified by the Council. But surely we should reconsider that situa-tion. If I may speak firmly as the current President, it is not the President's program but the Association's pro-gram, and we should see to it that the President's hand is steadied by suitable representation of the Association's multifarious interests, to protect ourselves from able, strong-willed, but quite parochial presidents (a highly probable combination of character traits). 

Let me now speak bluntly of certain political issues, though these are the matters that I should hope would be debated at considerable length in open conclave. (1) The proposals of the Fans Committee seek to reaffirm and restore membership participation and responsibility in the selection not only of governing mechanisms, but also of the process of nomination. I have heard some talk to the effect that this report is a method of consolidating the control of a clique or cabal or establishment. Read the proposals, please, with care, and then ask what bear-ing they have on such a suggestion. (2) No one wants to weaken regional societies, which have important func-tions to perform. I am an active member of my regional society. but I do not think of it as either a wholly-owned subsidiary of the ASA, or, on the other hand, as con-stituting a "regional bloc" in ASA decisions. Most of our reasonable differences within the ASA have little to do with geography: preferences in style of sociological work, views on the selection and accountability of technical officers of the Association, scientism versus activism as the proper stance of the sociologist. These issues cut deep, and will remain, but I doubt that they have any sub-stantial relevance to the operation of regional groups. I hope that regional societies will not get organizationally more closely integrated with the ASA, other than through the advisory committee proposed here. Let pluralism pre-vail. (3) 1 believe we should continue and perhaps ex-pand the recognition of affiliated societies, primarily as a basis of program cooperation. This year in Chicago not only did the Society for the Stud )' of Social Problems 

> The American Sociologist

meet just prior to the Association's convention, as usual, but so did the Rural Sociological Society and the Anier-jean Catholic Sociological Society. So, in effect, did the newly formed Law and Society Association. The Sociolog-ical Research Association always meets at the time of the Association's convention but does not appear on the prograni. As long as the actual governing of the Associa-tion is not at issue, program cooperation with separately organized groups would seem mutually beneficial. 

I promised to be blunt, and I have fulfilled that promise. But let me he more positive: let us have all sorts of associations that represent identifiable common in-terests.'and let those associations have their own ways of finding what unites them. But let us have an American Sociological Association, with a membership that is entirely individual, dedicated only to our common con-cerns as sociologists, and not filtered through regional identification, ideological stands, or substantive spe-cialties. 

Now, let me say a word about procedure. I propose the following: During this year Dr. Edmund Volkart, the Association's Executive Officer, and I hope to meet with every regional society in an open membership meeting. We hope to be joined in those sessions by the one or more members of the regional association who served on the Committee on Organizational Relationships, members who can therefore therefore testify concerning the "legislative history" of particular proposals. Subsequent to these regional meetings, but before the 1966 Annual Meeting, I hope it will he possible for the current Council of the American Sociological Association to meet in extra-ordinary session, undisturbed b y other business, for full discussion of the proposals, point by point. 

In addition to the invitation extended by the Editor 

of The American Sociologist to submit comients for possible publication in this journal, I should welcome expression of view's from an )' member of the Association to inc personally. You may address me at Russell Sage Foundation, 230 Park Avenue, New York, N.Y. 10017. I cannot promise an extended bilateral correspondence, as time and energy have their limits. But I can promise referral to lii)' superiors, the membership of the Council of this Association. 

All changes in the Constitution and By-laws, recoin-mended b y the Council, will, in accord with the provi-sions of the Constitution. be submitted to vote by the entire voting membership of the Association. 

As sociologists we must, of course, understand that things fit together—else we are out of business—but this comment is not meant to dissuade debate on proposals, one by one, as long as some suitable sense is exercised relating to the context of the organizational plans as a whole. I am not equally enthusiastic about all of the pro-posals of this plan, but I have been impressed by the good sense and sociological wisdom that has gone into this report. 

The reforms proposed in this report offer the chance that we can not only hold together as a sociological fraternity, despite the many intellectual, ideological, and merely technical issues that divide us, but also advance to a more effective role as a learned society. The report makes sense to me as contributing to that end, by many of us devoutly desired. 

I hope that we may, once more, find the highest rather than the lowest common denominator in our discussions. May I entreat you as a colleague in our common con-cerns to view these proposals in that light.
